Libraries / price_action
price_action · structural feature library · documentation

Price Action

A Python library that turns an OHLCV dataframe into descriptive structural features: candle anatomy, two swing engines (fractal and zigzag), market-structure grammar, breaks of structure and changes of character, fair value gaps and order blocks — as events and as zone tables with a mitigation life-cycle — breaker blocks, liquidity sweeps, equal highs and lows, the premium/discount dealing range and the OTE band, classic chart patterns, horizontal levels and diagonal trendlines. Every detector is non-repainting. Built on pandas and numpy only.

6 modules 38 functions + 13 utility names non-repainting v0.3.0 source 37730ca python 3.12+ pandas · numpy
Scope

Every output is a research feature, not a trading signal. The library is not a buy/sell system, not a strategy framework, not a backtester, and not financial advice. It extracts geometric price-action / smart-money-concept features for research pipelines; no output carries any claim of predictive value.

The PAResult contract

Every detector takes an OHLCV dataframe — plus, for the structure-dependent detectors, the result it builds on: a swings frame, or a level, trendline or zone table — and returns a PAResult, a small slotted dataclass whose three fields are type-checked at construction (a wrong type raises TypeError). The candle-anatomy primitives are the one family that returns something else: a bare float64 Series.

import price_action as pa

df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)        # synthetic and seeded, not market data
swings = pa.detect_swings(df, left=3, right=3)
swings.name        # "swings"
swings.values      # DataFrame on df.index: swing_high, swing_low, swing_high_price, swing_low_price
swings.metadata    # method="fractal", left, right, tie_handling, repaints=False, warm_up_bars=6, columns

levels = pa.detect_support_resistance(df, swings)
levels.values      # TABLE on a fresh RangeIndex: side, level_price, formed_at_pos, formed_at, touches
levels.metadata["output_format"]    # "level_table"
pa.detect_level_breakout(df, levels)    # a table consumer: per-bar events again
fieldtypewhat it holds
namestrDetector identifier, the key plot_price_action dispatches on. Usually the function name without detect_; three differ: classify_structure → "market_structure", detect_swings_zigzag → "zigzag_swings", detect_order_block_zones → "ob_zones"
valuesSeries | DataFramePer-bar output on the input index (warm-up and unknown bars NaN), or — for the five table detectors — one row per object on a fresh RangeIndex
metadatadictmethod, the parameters, repaints, the warm-up (warm_up_bars or warm_up) and the resolved columns map; a consumer nests its input's metadata under swings_metadata, levels_metadata, trendlines_metadata or zones_metadata

Across the package there are three output shapes — the first of them outside that container — and a consumer has to know which one it is holding:

  • Primitive series — body_size, candle_range, upper_wick, lower_wick and the three range-normalised ratios live in price_action.candles (they are not re-exported at the top level) and return a plain float64 Series on the input index: no PAResult, no metadata. They resolve column names but do not dtype-validate; a NaN input propagates, and the ratios are NaN on a flat candle (high == low).
  • Per-bar event frame — 26 of the 31 detectors. The four candle detectors return a single Series named after the detector, the rest a DataFrame; either way the index is the input's, unsorted and unmodified. Event columns are float64 1.0/0.0/NaN, never bool; candle_direction, and detect_engulfing / detect_pin_bar with direction="both", are signed 1.0/-1.0/0.0. Price columns (*_price, *_level, *_neckline, zone bounds) are NaN except at the event bar — with three state series as the exception: detect_range and detect_ote fill their bounds on every bar the state holds, and detect_premium_discount reports range_position on every measurable bar.
  • Object table — detect_support_resistance, detect_trendlines, detect_fvg_zones, detect_order_block_zones and detect_breaker_blocks return one frozen row per object on a fresh RangeIndex, with formed_at_pos (the int64 bar position in df where the object became knowable — positions, because index labels can repeat) and formed_at (the index label at that position, its dtype following df's index). The format is named in metadata["output_format"]. Rows are append-only in bar order and never revised. A table has no way to say "unknown", so where a per-bar detector would emit NaN a table emits no row; detect_fvg_zones and detect_order_block_zones record this in metadata["nan_policy"].
table (output_format)produced byone row perconsumed by
level_tabledetect_support_resistancehorizontal level: a cluster of min_touches same-side pivots, frozen at the confirmation that completed itdetect_level_breakout, detect_level_retest
trendline_tabledetect_trendlinessloped line from a consecutive same-side pivot pair, frozen at the second pivot's confirmation bardetect_trendline_breakout, detect_trendline_retest
fvg_zone_tabledetect_fvg_zonesthree-bar gap, or with join_consecutive=True a merged run of gapsdetect_fvg_mitigation

Tables are inputs, not end products. Every table consumer accepts the table's PAResult or its raw frame and validates only the columns its machine reads — side, level_price, formed_at_pos for levels; side, anchor2_pos, anchor2_price, slope, formed_at_pos for lines; side, upper, lower, formed_at_pos for zones — and tolerates extra columns. The three zone consumers therefore accept any of the three zone tables; the pairings above are the documented compositions, not the only legal ones. Levels and lines are active from formed_at_pos itself, zones from formed_at_pos + 1.

Non-repainting semantics

"Non-repainting" has a precise meaning here: the value at bar t is a function of bars ≤ t only, so appending bars never changes it. Every result stamps repaints: False in its metadata. The properties below are what that promise rests on, and two of them are worth keeping apart: every detector is prefix invariant, but only the few with a fixed warm-up and bounded history are offset invariant.

f(df.iloc[:k]) = f(df).iloc[:k]   — prefix (truncation) invariance: every per-bar detector
T(df.iloc[:k]) = T(df).iloc[:m]   — row-prefix invariance: the table analogue, swings recomputed on the prefix
f(df.iloc[s:]).iloc[w:] = f(df).iloc[s+w:]   — offset invariance: only fixed-warm-up detectors without unbounded history
  • Confirmation bar — an event is emitted at the bar where it becomes knowable, never stamped back onto an earlier bar. A fractal swing with right=r is emitted at t = p + r, where p is the pivot; a zigzag swing at the bar its retracement threshold is crossed; a break, sweep or order block at the bar whose close (or wick) confirms it; a reversal pattern at the first bar, from its arming bar on, whose price is beyond the neckline; a table row at the bar its object formed. (plot_price_action draws swing markers at the pivot for readability; the detection bar is still the confirmation bar.)
  • Fixed warm-up — metadata["warm_up_bars"] is an integer where one exists: 0 for candle_direction, detect_doji and detect_pin_bar, 1 for detect_engulfing, left + right for detect_swings (6 at the defaults), 2 for detect_fvg and for detect_fvg_zones in its default un-merged mode, and 1 for detect_swings_zigzag. All of them except the zigzag are offset invariant.
  • Data-dependent warm-up — every other detector records metadata["warm_up"] = "data_dependent": a per-bar channel is NaN until its question can be posed — enough confirmed swings (one of that side for a break, one of each side for the dealing range and the OTE leg, the min_count or min_swings of a cluster), the first level, line or zone of that side, the first armed pattern candidate — and 0.0/1.0 from then on, except on bars a detector declares unmeasurable (a degenerate dealing range or OTE leg, and detect_ote's inactive direction). The tables, which cannot hold NaN, simply have no row yet.
  • Unbounded history — the detectors that run a causal state machine over swings or over a table set metadata["unbounded_history"] = True: their state accumulates from the first swing or table row, so they are prefix invariant but not offset invariant. The zigzag is the one hybrid, carrying both warm_up_bars = 1 and unbounded_history = True, because its running extremum reaches back to the previous pivot. detect_fvg_zones(join_consecutive=True) joins this group, since a run of merged gaps has no length bound; in its default mode it records unbounded_history = False, while the candle detectors, detect_swings and detect_fvg omit the key.
  • NaN means unknown — 0.0 is a decision, NaN is its absence: warm-up, or a needed input that is NaN. A NaN deciding price leaves the machine's state unchanged, so a pending break, retest or mitigation is delayed, never assumed missed (the one exception is detect_range, which abandons a would-be formation whose bar has a NaN deciding price). A NaN swing event is treated as no confirmation (metadata["nan_swing_policy"] = "treated_as_no_swing"), except in classify_structure, which reports that bar's channel as NaN ("unknown_bar_nan_output_state_preserved"). Tables cannot say unknown: detect_fvg_zones records "nan_input_bars_emit_no_row", detect_order_block_zones "nan_or_degenerate_or_not_found_bars_emit_no_row", and detect_fvg remains the NaN-aware view of the same gaps.
  • Columns — detectors address columns by canonical name (open, high, low, close, volume). The columns argument, a ColumnMap, maps canonical names to the frame's own labels; omitted names map to themselves, several names may alias one column, an unknown canonical key is a ValueError, and the resolved map is recorded in metadata["columns"]. OHLC is required everywhere, even where only high and low are read; volume is required only by detect_order_block_zones, and not even there with volume_window=None.
  • Validation errors — a missing required column raises MissingColumnError (it carries .missing and .required); an empty frame raises InsufficientDataError. Every detector asks for at least one row and nothing more, so a frame shorter than the warm-up is not an error: it returns NaN. A non-numeric, bool or complex required column raises TypeError; a duplicated required column label, an out-of-range or unknown parameter (a few type checks raise TypeError instead), and a malformed swings or table input (a missing column, a swings index that is not df's index, a confirmed swing with a NaN price, a zone with upper <= lower) raise ValueError. Candle consistency (high >= max(open, close) and so on) is checked only on request, through validate_ohlcv(check_sanity=True); no detector turns it on.
  • Bars, not time — left, right, min_swings, atr_window, volume_window, formed_at_pos and a trendline's slope (price per bar position) all count bars of whatever timeframe is fed in. The library never sorts the index or checks its spacing: duplicate or unsorted indexes are the caller's responsibility.

Two swing engines, one contract

Almost everything above the candle layer is built on swings — sixteen detectors take a swings frame as input — and two engines produce one. detect_swings is the fractal definition: a pivot must strictly exceed its left neighbours behind and its right neighbours ahead, so it confirms on a fixed schedule. detect_swings_zigzag is the threshold-reversal definition: the running extremum since the last pivot confirms once price retraces reversal away from it, measured on wicks, so it confirms whenever the retracement happens.

detect_swingsdetect_swings_zigzag
name · method"swings" · "fractal""zigzag_swings" · "reversal_threshold"
parametersleft=3, right=3reversal=0.05, strictly between 0 and 1
swing highhigh[p] strictly above the left highs before and the right highs afterthe running maximum since the last pivot, confirmed at the first bar with low[t] <= max · (1 − reversal)
emissiont = p + right, a fixed delaythe crossing bar; the delay varies (0 to 13 bars for highs, 0 to 17 for lows on the 500-bar sample)
pivot positionderived: t − rightpublished: swing_high_pos / swing_low_pos
tiesstrict: an equal neighbour kills the swingthe earliest bar of equal extremes is the pivot
sequencehigh and low channels independentlegs alternate strictly: high, low, high
warm-upwarm_up_bars = left + right; offset invariantwarm_up_bars = 1 and unbounded_history = True; not offset invariant
NaN inputa NaN high (low) anywhere in the pivot window makes the high (low) channel NaN at its confirmation bara bar with a NaN high or low is skipped whole; state is kept

The widely circulated zigzag stamps each pivot onto the bar of the extremum — a marker written into the past, which moves when a later bar prints a new extreme. This engine keeps the concept and drops the retro-stamping: the event lands on the bar the threshold is crossed, and the extremum's location travels in the data. That is the one thing the zigzag adds to the contract. Because a variable delay cannot be inverted, it publishes the pivot's bar position as two extra float64 columns, NaN off events, and records metadata["position_columns"] = True. Before the first pivot both candidates run, and a single bar wide enough to cross both thresholds is resolved by its close direction — a bar that closed up completed the swing low, one that closed down the swing high, an exact doji neither.

The four core columns mean the same thing in both engines, so every swings consumer — classify_structure, detect_bos, detect_choch, detect_liquidity_sweep, detect_order_blocks, detect_order_block_zones, detect_equal_levels, detect_premium_discount, detect_ote, the five pattern detectors, detect_support_resistance and detect_trendlines — accepts either engine's PAResult or its raw values frame. detect_trendlines is the one consumer that needs pivot positions: it reads the position columns when both are present (metadata["position_source"] = "pos_columns", metadata["right"] = None), and otherwise derives them as t − right, taking right from a fractal PAResult's metadata or, for a raw fractal frame, from an explicit right= argument. A right supplied alongside the position columns, or only one of the two columns, raises ValueError: two contradictory position sources are refused rather than reconciled.

zz = pa.detect_swings_zigzag(df, reversal=0.05)
zz.values.columns    # the four swing columns + swing_high_pos, swing_low_pos
pa.detect_bos(df, zz)                         # any swings consumer takes either engine
pa.detect_trendlines(df, zz).metadata["position_source"]   # "pos_columns"
pa.detect_trendlines(df, swings.values, right=3)       # raw fractal frame: right= is required

Neither engine is the right one; they disagree by construction. On the 500-bar sample the fractal engine at (3, 3) confirms 39 swing highs and 43 swing lows, the zigzag at 5% confirms 17 of each. Fractal swings are scale-free and answer on a fixed schedule; threshold swings answer to how far price actually moved. Which one describes a market better is a question for the research layer, and the library does not answer it.

The zone life-cycle

Three smc detectors emit a zone table instead of a per-bar series: detect_fvg_zones (fvg_zone_table), detect_order_block_zones (ob_zone_table) and detect_breaker_blocks (breaker_zone_table). A zone is a frozen price band with a side and a formation bar: one row, columns side, upper, lower, formed_at_pos, formed_at, plus extras such as ob_pos, strength or origin_pos. Two kinds of consumer walk the bars over such a table: the zone-return machine behind detect_fvg_mitigation and detect_ob_mitigation (one private implementation, differing only in the output column prefix), and the full-break test in detect_breaker_blocks, whose output is itself a zone table and can be fed back into the zone-return machine. The level and trendline tables follow the same frozen-table discipline but run machines of their own (levels, trendlines).

import price_action as pa

swings   = pa.detect_swings(df)
zones    = pa.detect_order_block_zones(df, swings)          # formed at the break bar
returns  = pa.detect_ob_mitigation(df, zones, mode="half")  # first return to the midpoint
breakers = pa.detect_breaker_blocks(df, zones)              # full break, side flipped
retests  = pa.detect_ob_mitigation(df, breakers, mode="touch")  # breaker retest

Formation. A row is written at the bar where its zone becomes knowable and is never modified afterwards. For a fair value gap that is the gap's third bar, or, with join_consecutive=True, the bar at which the run of merged gaps breaks — the first bar that adds no contiguous same-side gap to it. For an order block it is the break bar — the bar whose close (or wick) confirmed the structural break — while the order-block candle's own position travels separately as ob_pos. For a breaker it is the flip bar, with the source block's formed_at_pos carried as origin_pos. A bar whose answer is unknown — NaN inputs, or an order-block scan that met a NaN open/close — emits no row, since a table has no shape for "unknown". A decided order block whose bounds are NaN or degenerate is omitted too, because the downstream machines would reject it. Every row a library detector emits therefore has two non-NaN bounds with upper > lower.

Activation at formed_at_pos + 1. Both machines first judge a zone on the bar after its formation bar; the mitigation detectors record this as metadata["activation"] = "formation_bar_plus_one" (the breaker table's metadata carries no such key, but its flip search starts at the same bar). The formation bar is the bar at which the zone became knowable, and it is generally already in contact with its own band or running away from it: a bullish gap's upper is the formation bar's low, an order block's formation bar is the break that ran away from it, and a breaker's flip bar is the bar that closed (or wicked) beyond the zone it flips. Mitigation and breaking describe what price does afterwards, so the formation bar is excluded by one uniform rule with no special cases — including for a merged join_consecutive row, whose formation bar is the bar its run broke on. That break bar is not one of the run's own gap bars and can itself reach into, or through, the merged zone; under the uniform rule a fill on that bar is not counted, and only a later return mitigates the zone. The level and trendline machines differ here: a level or line is active on its own formation bar.

modebullish zone (judged by low[t])bearish zone (judged by high[t])level column carries
"touch"low < upper (strict)high > lower (strict)the near edge
"half"low ≤ (upper + lower) / 2high ≥ (upper + lower) / 2the midpoint
"full" (default)low ≤ lowerhigh ≥ upperthe far edge

Mitigation and consumption. A bullish zone sits below price and is mitigated when price comes back down into it; a bearish zone sits above and is mitigated on the way up. touch is strict because reaching a zone's own edge is not yet being inside it; half and full are inclusive because they name a depth to be reached. Each zone is tracked independently, mitigates at most once and is then consumed; later returns into it fire nothing. There is no cap on how many zones a side carries and no expiry, so an unconsumed zone stays live for the rest of the data.

  • first_formed — when several zones of one side are reached on the same bar the event is 1.0 and the level column carries the threshold of the first-formed zone (metadata["level_pick"] = "first_formed"). The machine reads "first-formed" as table-row order, which is formation order for every table the library emits and the defined meaning for a hand-built one.
  • NaN deciding price — the bar's event is NaN and the zone state is unchanged: a pending mitigation is delayed, never assumed missed.
  • Warm-up — per side, NaN before that side's earliest activation bar (or throughout if the side has no zones); from then on 0.0 on every decided bar, even when every zone has been consumed.
  • Validation — the table is checked for content, not only dtypes: a known side, an integer, present, non-negative formed_at_pos, numeric non-NaN bounds and upper > lower; a violation raises ValueError. Extra columns are tolerated, and a position at or beyond the end of df is legal and inert — exactly what replaying a full-data table against a shorter frame produces.

Breakers: a full break flips the zone. detect_breaker_blocks asks a different question of the same order-block table. From formed_at_pos + 1 on, a bullish zone breaks at the first bar whose close (break_mode="close", default) or low ("wick") lies strictly below lower; a bearish zone at the first close or high strictly above upper. Each zone flips at most once, and a bar whose deciding price is NaN takes no decision — the zone survives it and can flip later. The flipped row keeps the source bounds under the opposite side: a broken bullish block becomes a bearish zone. In close mode the flip bar's close sits below it; in wick mode only the flip bar's low is guaranteed to. Because that row satisfies the zone-table contract, a breaker retest is simply the zone-return machine run over the breaker table, detect_ob_mitigation(df, breakers, mode="touch"): the bearish geometry applies unchanged (a return up into the band, judged by high), and activation is the flip bar + 1. The two consumers keep separate state, so a zone can be mitigated in one and broken in the other. On OHLC-consistent candles a close below lower implies a low below it, so a mode="full" mitigation run over the same order-block table has already fired for every breaker's source zone at or before its flip bar.

Append-only, never converging. Rows are frozen at emission and appended in bar order, so the table computed on a prefix df.iloc[:k] is an exact row-prefix of the full-data table — the table form of non-repainting. The events built on a table are truncation invariant for the same reason: a decision at bar t reads bars up to t only and is never revised. They are not offset invariant, because the machine holds every unconsumed zone indefinitely: a computation started later never learns the zones that formed before its start, and no finite tail of history is guaranteed to reproduce the full-history event at a bar. On the library's 500-bar synthetic sample (load_sample_ohlcv(), default detect_fvg_zones table) with mode="full", one fair value gap was mitigated 192 bars after it formed and 23 of 155 gap zones were still live at the last bar. Every lifecycle detector therefore reports unbounded_history = True with a data-dependent warm-up.

Two representations, one definition — detect_fvg / detect_fvg_zones and detect_order_blocks / detect_order_block_zones each share one private implementation, so a table row and its per-bar event never disagree on bounds. Where "no object" and "unknown" must be told apart, read the per-bar detector; the table only ever carries decided objects.

The sample dataset

Every chart below shows the detector run on the library's own load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500) — a deterministic, seeded synthetic OHLCV frame. It is not market data, which is exactly why it is good documentation material: the events are reproducible on your machine with two lines of code. The price panel shows the close line inside the high–low envelope; events are drawn in green (bullish), red (bearish), or teal (neutral). Five detectors fire rarely or never at their defaults on these 500 bars; their charts use the parameters named in the caption and give the count at defaults.

candles

Bar anatomy — bodies, wicks, and canonical patterns · 11 functions

A candle is the atomic unit of price action: four prices that summarise one bar. The candlestick tradition — Japanese in origin, brought into Western technical analysis in the early 1990s — reads its anatomy. The body (open to close) is the bar's net result; the wicks (the range beyond the body) are the excursions that were reached and not held. A large body with small wicks is read as conviction, a small body with long wicks as indecision or rejection. The library measures the anatomy and leaves the reading to the caller.

body = |close − open|   — net movement of the bar
range = high − low   ·   upper wick = high − max(open, close)   ·   lower wick = min(open, close) − low
ratio = part / range   — body or wick share of the bar; NaN on a flat candle (high = low)

The module has two layers. The primitives — body_size, candle_range, upper_wick, lower_wick, body_ratio, upper_wick_ratio, lower_wick_ratio — are plain float64 Series on the input index, imported from price_action.candles rather than the top-level package. They resolve column names but do not validate dtypes; that is the detectors' job. The four detectors return a PAResult holding a per-bar Series: candle_direction (+1 when close > open, −1 when below, 0 when equal); detect_doji (a body no larger than body_threshold × range, default 0.1); detect_pin_bar (one dominant wick of at least min_wick_ratio of the range, default 0.66, a body of at most 0.25 and an opposite wick of at most 0.2 — bullish when the dominant wick is the lower one); and detect_engulfing, the one two-bar pattern: a bar of the opposite colour to its predecessor whose body covers the predecessor's body, or whose high/low covers the predecessor's range with method="range".

Every definition is a parameter, not folklore. Strict versus lenient engulfment is the strict flag; pin-bar thresholds are validated so the dominant wick must exceed what the opposite wick is allowed to be (overlapping thresholds raise ValueError, since a symmetric bar would otherwise qualify both ways). Two edge rules are deliberate and opposite: a flat candle is a doji (its zero body is within body_threshold times a zero range) but is 0.0 as a pin bar, because its ratios are undefined. direction picks the output form: "bullish" or "bearish" gives a clean 0.0/1.0 event series, "both" (the default) a signed 1.0/-1.0/0.0 series meant for comparators.

The detectors are context-free: each candle is judged against its own range, and engulfing against the bar before it, never against an average of recent bars as TA-Lib's CDL* functions do. Warm-up is zero bars, one for engulfing; any NaN in a needed price makes that bar NaN; and every detector is offset invariant. Nothing else in the library consumes this module — the structure, pattern and smart-money layers are built on swings or on raw bar geometry, not on candle labels.

When to reach for this module: bar-level features — continuous body and wick geometry, and the three canonical formations as reproducible, context-free predicates for a research pipeline.

candle_direction

from price_action import candle_direction

candle_direction(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Signed body direction of each candle.

Emits 1.0 when close > open (bullish body), -1.0 when close < open (bearish body), and 0.0 when close == open. There is no warm-up. A bar with a NaN open or close is emitted as NaN.

Event-series convention: this is a signed 1.0/-1.0/0.0 series, not a binary 0.0/1.0 event stream. It is meant for comparator use (feeding a directional sign into other detectors); consumers that expect a clean binary event series should derive one themselves (e.g. compare against a target sign).

detect_doji

from price_action import detect_doji

detect_doji(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    body_threshold: float = 0.1,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Flag doji candles: a body that is small relative to the range.

A bar is a doji (1.0) when body_size <= body_threshold * range, else 0.0. A flat candle (open == high == low == close) has body_size == 0 and range == 0, so 0 <= threshold * 0 holds and the bar is flagged as a doji. (This is the opposite convention to detect_pin_bar, which treats a flat candle as not a pin bar; the asymmetry is deliberate — a zero-body candle is the archetypal doji.) A bar with any NaN OHLC input is emitted as NaN.

detect_engulfing

from price_action import detect_engulfing

detect_engulfing(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    direction: str = 'both',
    method: str = 'body',
    strict: bool = True,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Flag two-bar engulfing patterns.

A bullish engulfing needs a bearish prior candle (close_prev < open_prev) followed by a bullish candle (close > open) whose body (or range) covers the prior candle's; a bearish engulfing is the mirror image. SMC definitions vary, so the covering rule and the compared span are both parameters and are recorded in the metadata.

  • method="body" compares the current body edges (open/close) against the previous body edges. method="range" compares the current high/low against the previous high/low.
  • strict=True requires strict inequalities on the covering comparisons; strict=False allows equality (<=/>=).

The first bar is NaN (one bar of warm-up). Any bar whose own or prior required OHLC inputs are NaN is emitted as NaN.

Event-series convention: direction="bullish" and direction="bearish" emit a clean 0.0/1.0 event series (integration-friendly for registries and comparators that expect binary events); direction="both" emits a signed 1.0/-1.0/0.0 series (bullish/bearish/neither) meant for comparator use, not a binary event stream.

detect_pin_bar

from price_action import detect_pin_bar

detect_pin_bar(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    direction: str = 'both',
    min_wick_ratio: float = 0.66,
    max_body_ratio: float = 0.25,
    max_opposite_wick_ratio: float = 0.2,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Flag pin bars (single dominant wick with a small body).

A bullish pin bar has a dominant lower wick: lower_wick_ratio >= min_wick_ratio and body_ratio <= max_body_ratio and upper_wick_ratio <= max_opposite_wick_ratio. A bearish pin bar is the mirror (dominant upper wick).

min_wick_ratio must be strictly greater than max_opposite_wick_ratio: the dominant wick has to be longer than the opposite wick is allowed to be. If the two thresholds overlapped, a symmetric bar (two long wicks of equal length) could satisfy both the bullish and the bearish conditions at once and the signed classification would be ambiguous, so overlapping thresholds raise ValueError.

A flat candle (high == low) has undefined ratios but is definitively not a pin bar, so it is emitted as 0.0 — NaN is reserved for genuinely missing input data. (This is the opposite convention to detect_doji, which flags a flat candle as a doji; the asymmetry is deliberate.) A bar with any NaN OHLC input is emitted as NaN.

Event-series convention: direction="bullish" and direction="bearish" emit a clean 0.0/1.0 event series (integration-friendly for registries and comparators that expect binary events); direction="both" emits a signed 1.0/-1.0/0.0 series (bullish/bearish/neither) meant for comparator use, not a binary event stream.

structure

Fractal and threshold swings, trend grammar, breaks of structure · 5 functions

Market structure is the skeleton of a price chart, and its joints are swing points — local extremes price carved out and left behind. Two definitions dominate the practice. Bill Williams' fractal marks a bar whose high stands above its neighbours on both sides; the zigzag marks an extreme once price has reversed a fixed percentage away from it. Both share a timing problem that is easy to hide: a swing high is not a swing high until the bars after it have printed lower, so any series that marks it on the extreme's own bar has used the future. Here every swing is emitted on its confirmation bar, and everything built on swings inherits that rule.

fractal swing high at p ⇔ high[p] > high[p−i] (i = 1…left) and high[p] > high[p+j] (j = 1…right)   — emitted at t = p + right
zigzag swing high at t ⇔ low[t] ≤ M · (1 − reversal), M = running max since the last pivot   — pivot bar carried in swing_high_pos
BOS ⇔ close breaks the last confirmed swing level in the direction of the previous break (or before any break)   — CHoCH ⇔ against it

The module has two swing engines behind one output contract (see the engines section). detect_swings is the fractal one, with strict inequalities on both sides (an equal neighbour kills the swing), a fixed delay of right bars and a warm-up of left + right. detect_swings_zigzag follows the running extremum since the last pivot and confirms it when price retraces reversal (default 5%) on the wicks; its delay varies, legs alternate strictly, and because the pivot's bar cannot be derived from the confirmation bar it publishes that bar in swing_high_pos / swing_low_pos. Both emit the same four core columns — the event flags and the pivot prices — so every structure consumer below accepts either.

classify_structure speaks the four-word grammar of trend. Each newly confirmed swing high is compared with the previous one — strictly higher is a higher high, strictly lower a lower high — and swing lows likewise give higher low and lower low. An equal price fires nothing but becomes the next reference; the first swing of each channel only seeds it. The two channels are independent and each is NaN until its first swing confirms.

detect_bos and detect_choch slice two views out of one break machine. It holds the most recent confirmed swing-high and swing-low levels and its own direction, set by the last break. An up break is a close strictly above the swing-high level (the high, with break_mode="wick"); it is a break of structure when the direction was already up or not yet set — the first break ever is a BOS by convention — and a change of character when it was down. Down breaks mirror this. A broken level is consumed until a new swing of that side confirms, the level is emitted beside the event, and a bar that breaks both levels emits both, its final direction taken from its body. The machine's direction comes from breaks alone: it does not read classify_structure's higher-high / higher-low grammar, which is computed independently. On the 500-bar sample with default fractal swings it finds 19 breaks of structure and 10 changes of character.

All five detectors are prefix invariant. Only detect_swings is also offset invariant: the zigzag's running extremum reaches back to the previous pivot, and the classifiers' references carry state from the first swing onward. All four record unbounded_history = True — the zigzag beside its one-bar warm_up_bars = 1, the three swing consumers with a data-dependent warm-up. A NaN swing event leaves the consumers' state untouched — classify_structure reports that channel as NaN at the bar, while the break machine still decides on a clean price.

When to reach for this module: the structural skeleton — where the confirmed extremes are on a fixed or a retracement schedule, which way the swing sequence is stepping, and the bars where price broke the last confirmed level with or against the direction of the previous break.

classify_structuredetect_bosdetect_chochdetect_swingsdetect_swings_zigzag

classify_structure

from price_action import classify_structure

classify_structure(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Classify each confirmed swing as a higher/lower high or low.

Walking the bars in order, the classifier tracks the price of the last confirmed swing high and the last confirmed swing low. At every bar where a swing high confirms (swing_high == 1.0), its pivot price is compared (strictly) against the previous confirmed swing high:

  • strictly higher -> higher_high fires (1.0) at that bar;
  • strictly lower -> lower_high fires;
  • equal -> neither fires (tie handling is "strict"), but the new swing still becomes the reference for the next comparison.

The first swing high ever seen has nothing to compare against, so it fires nothing but seeds the reference. Swing lows are classified the same way into higher_low / lower_low. The high and low channels are independent.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns higher_high, lower_high, higher_low, lower_low:

  • NaN before that channel's first confirmed swing (the classification question is not yet posed — the highs channel stays NaN until the first swing high confirms, the lows channel until the first swing low);
  • from that first confirmation onward, 1.0 at qualifying confirmation bars and 0.0 otherwise;
  • NaN at any bar where that side's swing event itself is NaN (unknown confirmation), leaving the running reference unchanged.

Note the contrast with the break machine behind detect_bos / detect_choch: both preserve state across a NaN swing event, but this classifier emits NaN at such a bar (policy "unknown_bar_nan_output_state_preserved"), whereas the break machine still emits definite 0.0/1.0 events when the deciding price is clean (policy "treated_as_no_swing").

Warm-up is therefore data-dependent, and the classifier has unbounded history (its state accumulates from the first swing), so it is truncation invariant but not offset invariant.

columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.

Output columns

detect_bos

from price_action import detect_bos

detect_bos(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect breaks of structure over confirmed swings.

An upward break of the last confirmed swing-high level is a BOS up when the trend direction is already up (+1) or not yet established (0 — the first break ever is labelled BOS by convention); a downward break of the last confirmed swing-low level mirrors this. A break that reverses the prevailing direction is a change of character, not a BOS, and is emitted by detect_choch instead — both run the same underlying machine.

Breaks use strict inequalities. In break_mode="close" an up break needs close > last_high and a down break close < last_low; in break_mode="wick" the bar's high / low are used instead. A bar that breaks both levels at once emits both events; its final direction follows the candle body (close vs open), and bos_level then carries the level of the side matching that direction (up on a doji tie).

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has three float64 columns:

  • bos_up / bos_down — 1.0 at BOS bars, 0.0 otherwise, NaN before the first confirmed level of that side exists and on bars whose deciding price is NaN (state is preserved across such bars);
  • bos_level — the broken level's price at BOS bars, NaN elsewhere.

Warm-up is data-dependent and the detector has unbounded history (the structural state accumulates from the first swing), so it is truncation invariant but not offset invariant.

detect_swings

from price_action import detect_swings

detect_swings(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    left: int = 3,
    right: int = 3,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect fractal swing highs and lows, emitted at their confirmation bar.

A bar p is a swing high iff high[p] > high[p - i] for every i in 1..left and high[p] > high[p + j] for every j in 1..right — strict inequalities on both sides, so a tie (an equal neighbouring high) kills the swing. Equal highs are deliberately not swings here; they matter later for equal-highs/liquidity detection, which is a separate detector. A swing low is the mirror condition on low with <.

Because a swing high is only knowable right bars after the pivot, the event is emitted at the confirmation bar t = p + right; the pivot sits at t - right. This makes the detector non-repainting: the value at bar t is computable from bars <= t and never changes when future bars are appended.

right=0 is legal (the pivot is confirmed on its own bar, still non-repainting since no future bars are consulted), but small right yields noisy swings.

The values DataFrame shares the input index and has exactly four float64 columns:

  • swing_high: 1.0 if a swing high is confirmed at bar t (pivot at t - right), 0.0 if no confirmation, NaN during warm-up or when the decision cannot be made because a needed input is NaN.
  • swing_low: the same for lows.
  • swing_high_price: at confirmation bars, the pivot's high value (high[t - right]); NaN everywhere else, warm-up included.
  • swing_low_price: the mirror.

The first left + right bars are warm-up: no pivot can be confirmed there, so every event column is NaN. The decision at confirmation bar t examines the window [p - left, p + right] (p = t - right); if any needed value in that window is NaN the corresponding event column is NaN (unknown) and its price column stays NaN. 0.0 therefore means "definitely no swing", distinct from NaN ("unknown"). The high and low channels are independent: a NaN low never affects a swing-high decision, and vice versa.

Parameters

leftint3Number of preceding bars a pivot must strictly exceed. Must be >= 1.
rightint3Number of following bars a pivot must strictly exceed, and the confirmation lag. Must be >= 0.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "swings" whose values is the four-column DataFrame described above.

Output columns

swing_lowevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)

detect_swings_zigzag

from price_action import detect_swings_zigzag

detect_swings_zigzag(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    reversal: float = 0.05,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect swing points by relative-threshold reversal, non-repainting.

A single causal pass tracks a running extremum — the candidate pivot — and confirms it the moment price retraces reversal away from it:

  • a swing high candidate is the running maximum of high since the last confirmed pivot; it confirms at the first bar t with low[t] <= running_max_price * (1 - reversal);
  • a swing low candidate is the running minimum of low; it confirms at the first bar with high[t] >= running_min_price * (1 + reversal).

The retracement is measured on wicks (the bar's low against a high candidate, its high against a low candidate), recorded as metadata["retrace_basis"] = "wick". A close-based variant — which would confirm later and less often — is deliberately left as future work rather than smuggled in behind the same name.

Intra-bar order. At each bar the candidates are updated first, then the confirmation is tested. A wide bar can therefore set a new running maximum and confirm that very maximum with its own low on the same bar. The running maximum advances only on a strictly greater high, so a run of equal highs keeps the earliest one as the pivot position (mirror for lows). Ties are invisible in the price columns but decide the position columns, hence metadata["tie_handling"] = "earliest_extremum".

Legs alternate strictly. Confirming a swing high starts a down leg: the confirming bar seeds the new low candidate at (low[t], t), the high candidate is dropped, and only a swing low can confirm next. Before the first pivot the direction is unknown, so both candidates run from bar 0 and either side may confirm. At most one pivot is confirmed per bar.

The pre-first-pivot both-cross bar. While the direction is still unknown, one very wide bar can cross both thresholds at once. It is resolved by the bar's own close direction, which says which move happened last: close > open means the bar ended on the up-move, so the rise from the low candidate came last and the swing low confirms; close < open confirms the swing high; an exact doji (close == open) confirms nothing and keeps both candidates alive — the conservative reading, since the bar carries no evidence either way. Once a leg is active only one threshold is watched, so the case cannot recur.

The values DataFrame shares the input index and has exactly six float64 columns:

  • swing_high / swing_low: 1.0 at a confirmation bar, 0.0 when no confirmation is possible there, NaN when the decision cannot be made. Identical in meaning to the fractal detector's columns.
  • swing_high_price / swing_low_price: at a confirmation bar, the confirmed pivot's price (the running extremum, not the confirming bar's price); NaN everywhere else.
  • swing_high_pos / swing_low_pos: at a confirmation bar, the pivot's integer bar position as a float64; NaN everywhere else. Bar positions are exact integers far below 2**53, so the float64 round-trip is lossless. Recorded as metadata["position_columns"] = True.

Warm-up is exactly one bar. Bar 0 initialises the candidates and never confirms (both event columns are NaN there); decisions start at bar 1. That is the only fixed warm-up: the running extremum reaches back to the last pivot, arbitrarily far, so the result also carries metadata["unbounded_history"] = True — the detector is truncation invariant but not offset invariant.

NaN bars are skipped entirely. If high or low is NaN at bar t, both event columns are NaN there and the state is fully preserved: no candidate update, no confirmation test. A pivot established before the gap still confirms after it, carrying its original position. The one further NaN case is a pre-first-pivot both-cross bar whose open or close is NaN: the tie cannot be broken, so both event columns are NaN rather than a confident 0.0, and nothing is confirmed.

The threshold is a relative fraction of the candidate price, so it assumes prices are positive — as market prices are. On a series with non-positive prices the multiplicative band is not meaningful (the detector still runs and stays non-repainting, but the thresholds no longer describe a percentage retracement).

This is a feature extractor. A confirmed swing describes what price has already done; it makes no claim about what price will do next.

Parameters

dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. high and low drive the machine and open / close break the pre-first-pivot both-cross tie; the frame must satisfy the OHLC schema, and volume is optional.
reversalfloat0.05The retracement fraction that confirms a candidate (0.05 == 5%). Must be strictly between 0 and 1.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "zigzag_swings" whose values is the six-column DataFrame described above.

Output columns
swing_highevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
swing_lowevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
swing_high_pricelevel / position (NaN except where defined)
swing_low_pricelevel / position (NaN except where defined)
swing_high_poslevel / position (NaN except where defined)
swing_low_poslevel / position (NaN except where defined)
Raises
ValueErrorIf reversal is not strictly between 0 and 1 (NaN included).
Example

df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)

result = pa.detect_swings_zigzag(df)
result.name                         # "zigzag_swings"
result.metadata["repaints"]         # False
result.values[["swing_high", "swing_low"]].sum() # events on the sample data — swing_high: 17, swing_low: 17

smc

Smart-money footprints — imbalances, order blocks, liquidity, the dealing range · 11 functions

Smart-money concepts read a chart as a record of order flow too large to be filled at one price. Such flow is said to leave geometric traces: price ranges crossed so fast that they were never traded two-sided (imbalances), the last candle before a decisive break (the order block), pools of stop orders resting beyond obvious swing extremes (liquidity), and the position of price inside the range the market is currently dealing in. The narrative behind these terms is contested and their definitions vary from source to source; the geometry is not. This module implements one explicit reading per detector, records it in metadata["method"], and emits it as a descriptive feature. Whether a zone is later respected is not something any detector here claims to know.

The imbalance and the order block come in two representations. A per-bar event series answers "did it happen at this bar" and can say unknown with NaN. A zone table re-expresses the same objects as one frozen row each — side, bounds, formation bar — so that a gap or a block becomes an object with a lifetime that later detectors can track. The two representations of a concept share one private definition, so a table row and its per-bar event never disagree on bounds. The table omits what it cannot or will not carry — unknown (NaN) events and, for order blocks, a decided block whose bounds are NaN or degenerate — plus the optional gap merge described below. Lifecycle detectors complete the table side: they mark when price returns into a zone and when it breaks fully through one (see the zone life-cycle).

bullish FVG at t ⇔ low[t] − high[t−2] > 0 and ≥ min_gap_size — zone [high[t−2], low[t]], emitted at the third bar
bullish order block = last candle with close < open before an upward break — emitted at the break bar, not at the candle
breaker ⇔ close (or wick) strictly beyond the far edge at t ≥ formed_at_pos + 1 — same bounds, side flipped

Imbalance. A fair value gap is the three-bar void: bar t's low clears bar t−2's high (bullish), or its high stays below bar t−2's low (bearish), so the outer bars' ranges never overlapped. Both tests are strict on zero — touching candles leave no gap — and min_gap_size is in absolute price units. detect_fvg is the per-bar view: decided from bars t−2 … t alone, with a fixed two-bar warm-up, offset invariant, NaN wherever a needed input is NaN. detect_fvg_zones emits the same gaps as a table. With the default join_consecutive=False its rows correspond one-for-one to detect_fvg's event bars with identical bounds; a bar whose inputs are NaN, which detect_fvg reports as NaN, emits no row. join_consecutive=True merges same-side gaps on consecutive bars whose zones overlap or touch into one row spanning their union, emitted at the first bar where the run breaks: every emission, a lone gap included, arrives at least one bar later, a run still open at the end of the data emits nothing, and the mode carries unbounded history.

Order blocks. The last_opposite_candle method finds a block backwards from a structural break. The breaks come from the same causal machine as detect_bos / detect_choch; with require_bos=True (default) only BOS breaks anchor a block, with False CHoCH breaks anchor one too. From the break bar the detector scans strictly earlier bars for the most recent decisive opposite candle — close < open for a bullish block, close > open for a bearish one — skipping dojis and same-direction candles. The scan is unbounded: exhausting history yields 0.0, meeting a NaN open or close first yields NaN. The event lands on the break bar, where everything it describes is known, and the zone is the candle's [low, high] (zone="range", default) or its body. detect_order_block_zones runs the identical scan and writes one row per block: formed_at_pos is the break bar, ob_pos the candle itself, and a row whose bounds would be NaN or degenerate is omitted, so every row has two non-NaN bounds with upper > lower. Its strength column divides the candle's volume by the simple mean volume over the volume_window bars (default 20) ending at that candle — truncated at the start of history, NaN volumes excluded, volume_window=None to switch it off. It is a descriptive ratio, with no claim that a heavier block behaves differently.

Return and failure. detect_fvg_mitigation and detect_ob_mitigation run one zone-return machine and differ only in their column prefix. A bullish zone sits below price and is judged by low, a bearish zone by high, and mode sets how deep the return must go: "touch" (entry past the near edge, strict), "half" (the midpoint — the gap's "consequent encroachment", the block's "50% level") or "full" (default, the far edge); half and full are inclusive. A zone activates on the bar after its formation bar, mitigates at most once and is then consumed; when several zones of one side are reached on the same bar the event is 1.0 and the level column carries the first-formed zone's threshold. detect_breaker_blocks marks the order blocks price failed through: the first bar after formation whose close (break_mode="close", default) or wick lies strictly beyond the far edge flips the zone, once, and the row re-publishes the unchanged bounds under the opposite side, with origin_pos pointing back at the source. A touch is mitigation, not a break. Because the breaker output is itself a valid zone table, a breaker retest needs no detector of its own: detect_ob_mitigation(df, breakers, mode="touch").

EQH at t ⇔ a swing high confirms and its last min_count highs satisfy (max − min) ≤ tolerance · max(|max|, |min|) — the line is the max; EQL mirrors it with the min
range_position = (close − L) / (H − L) — L, H: last confirmed swing low and high; premium ⇔ > 0.5, discount ⇔ < 0.5
OTE band of an up leg = [H − r2 · R, H − r1 · R], R = H − L — (r1, r2) = (0.618, 0.79) by default

Liquidity. Stop orders are said to cluster beyond obvious extremes, and two detectors read that geometry. detect_liquidity_sweep tracks the last confirmed swing-high and swing-low prices — the levels the break machine watches. A bar whose high pierces the high level strictly while closing back at or below it is a sweep (wick_only=True, default); a close strictly through the level is a structural break, not a sweep, and consumes the level. A sweep never consumes it, so the same level can be swept repeatedly until a close goes through or a newer swing replaces it; with wick_only=False the pierce alone fires, and a close-through bar is then both a sweep and the level's consumption. detect_equal_levels marks equal highs and equal lows (EQH / EQL): the last min_count (default 2) consecutive same-side confirmed swings, equal within a relative tolerance (default 0.0005) under the max-spread rule. The reported line is the cluster's extreme — the maximum for EQH, the minimum for EQL — because the liquidity such a line describes rests outside the pivots; it is deliberately not the mean a support/resistance level is frozen at. A run of three or more re-fires at every confirmation from the min_count-th on, and the two sides warm up and answer independently.

Where inside the move. detect_premium_discount places each close in the dealing range between the last confirmed swing low and the last confirmed swing high, each edge replaced at the confirmation bar of a fresh same-side pivot. range_position is 0 at the low and 1 at the high and is not clamped: a close beyond an edge — typical right after a break, before the taken level is replaced — prints above 1 or below 0. premium and discount are the strictly open halves, so a close exactly at equilibrium (0.5) is in neither. All three columns are NaN until both edges have confirmed, on a degenerate or inverted range (the last swing low at or above the last swing high, reachable in choppy structure) and on a NaN close. detect_ote publishes the retracement band of the latest impulse leg. The order in which the last swing high and the last swing low confirmed names the leg — a swing high confirming after the swing low is an up impulse, and its bullish band is measured down from that high — a same-bar tie is broken by the bar's close direction, and the band is recomputed only at confirmations and frozen in between. It is a state series: the bounds are filled on every bar the leg is active, membership is inclusive at both edges, and every column is NaN on a degenerate leg. The name comes from the ICT literature; the detector draws a band and makes no claim about entering there.

Everything inherits the structure layer's discipline: confirmed swings only, emission at the bar where an object becomes knowable, tables append-only and row-prefix invariant. Apart from detect_fvg and the un-merged zone table, which look back a fixed two bars, every detector here is a causal state machine with unbounded_history = True — truncation invariant but not offset invariant, with a data-dependent warm-up — so a zone formed hundreds of bars earlier can still be mitigated or broken on the current bar.

When to reach for this module: footprint features with a lifetime — where imbalances and break-origin zones sit, when price returned into them or failed through them, where equal-highs and equal-lows lines and swept levels lie, and where the close sits inside the current swing range — as non-repainting event series, state series and frozen zone tables for research pipelines.

detect_breaker_blocks

from price_action import detect_breaker_blocks

detect_breaker_blocks(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    zones: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Emit one frozen table row per order-block zone that price broke through.

A bullish zone [lower, upper] becomes a bearish breaker at the first bar t >= formed_at_pos + 1 with close[t] < lower (break_mode="close", default) or low[t] < lower (break_mode="wick"); a bearish zone becomes a bullish breaker on close[t] > upper / high[t] > upper. Both comparisons are strict, a full traversal of the zone is required (a touch is mitigation, not a break), and each zone flips at most once. A bar with a NaN deciding price takes no decision at all — the zone survives it unconsumed and can flip later. See the module docstring for the activation rationale and the NaN/table doctrine.

Nothing here is a prediction. The SMC literature reads a breaker as "failed demand now acting as supply"; this function only reports the geometric event of a zone being fully traversed, with the side label flipped.

values is a pandas.DataFrame with a fresh pandas.RangeIndex (not df's index) and one row per flip:

  • side (str): the flipped side — "bearish" for a broken bullish order block, "bullish" for a broken bearish one.
  • upper / lower (float64): the source zone's bounds, unchanged.
  • formed_at_pos (int64): the position of the flip bar, where this row was emitted and became knowable.
  • formed_at: the df index label at formed_at_pos.
  • origin_pos (int64): the source zone's own formed_at_pos (its structural break bar), for traceability back to the order block.

Rows are frozen at emission and append-only in bar order — within one bar, in the source table's row (first-formed) order — so the table computed on a prefix df.iloc[:k] is an exact row-prefix of the full-data table, the table analogue of non-repainting.

Because the emitted table carries side / upper / lower / formed_at_pos, it is itself a valid input to detect_ob_mitigation, which is how a breaker retest is expressed:

.. code-block:: python

breakers = pa.detect_breaker_blocks(df, pa.detect_order_block_zones(df, sw))
retests = pa.detect_ob_mitigation(df, breakers, mode="touch")

zonesPAResult | pd.DataFrame—The PAResult from detect_order_block_zones, or a DataFrame carrying the side / upper / lower / formed_at_pos columns. Extra columns (ob_pos, strength, ...) are tolerated.
break_modestr'close'"close" (default) or "wick".
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "breaker_blocks".

Output columns table — one row per object

lowerfloat64
formed_at_posint64

Raises

Example
# df: OHLCV dataframe — here the library's own synthetic sample
import price_action as pa
df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)

swings = pa.detect_swings(df)
zones = pa.detect_order_block_zones(df, swings)
result = pa.detect_breaker_blocks(df, zones)
result.name                     # "breaker_blocks"

result.values.columns.tolist()  # ['side', 'upper', 'lower', 'formed_at_pos', 'formed_at', 'origin_pos']

detect_equal_levels

from price_action import detect_equal_levels

detect_equal_levels(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    tolerance: float = 0.0005,
    min_count: int = 2,
    side: str = 'both',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect equal highs / equal lows among consecutive confirmed swings.

Walking the bars in order, the detector keeps — per side — the last min_count confirmed pivot prices of that side. An EQH event fires at bar t iff a swing high confirms at t and those last min_count swing highs (this one included) are equal within tolerance under the max-spread rule this library uses for clustered swings:

(max - min) <= tolerance * max(abs(max), abs(min))

tolerance is a dimensionless relative fraction (0.0005 == 0.05%), so the admissible spread scales with the price level, and a spread landing exactly on the boundary qualifies (the test is <=). The EQL event is the mirror on swing lows.

"Consecutive" means adjacent in that side's confirmed-swing stream: no other swing of the same side confirmed in between (opposite-side swings in between are irrelevant, so the two sides are fully independent). A run of three or more equal swings therefore fires at each confirmation from the min_count-th onward: with min_count=2 a triple fires twice (bars 2 and 3 of the run), because the overlapping windows (1, 2) and (2, 3) both qualify. That re-firing is deliberate — each confirmation is a fresh piece of evidence for the same line, and a detector that suppressed it would have to decide when a run "ends", which is not knowable causally.

The reported line. eqh_level is the maximum of the qualifying cluster's pivot prices, not their mean: the liquidity an equal-highs line describes rests above the highs, so the outermost pivot is the price a consumer wants to draw and test against. eql_level mirrors it with the minimum. (The mean is a fair choice for a support/resistance band — which is why detect_support_resistance uses it — but a liquidity line is one-sided.)

The values DataFrame shares df's index, is all float64, and its columns depend on side:

  • "both": eqh, eqh_level, eql, eql_level;
  • "eqh" / "eql": only that side's event and level column.

Event columns carry 1.0 / 0.0 / NaN; a *_level column carries the line price at its side's event bars and NaN everywhere else.

NaN policy. A NaN swing event is treated as no confirmation (metadata["nan_swing_policy"] = "treated_as_no_swing"): it never enters the window, so the state is preserved and a later cluster still fires. Since that bar's answer for the side is genuinely unknown — a confirmation there might have completed a cluster — the side's columns are NaN at that bar. Warm-up is NaN per side until min_count swings of that side have ever confirmed; from that bar on the side emits 0.0 on every non-event bar (swing confirmations that do not cluster and bars with no swing at all). The latch never reverts: the window can only be refreshed, never emptied.

Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Only its index and column schema are used here — every decision comes from the swing pivots.
swingsPAResult | pd.DataFrame—The PAResult from detect_swings, or its raw values frame. Must carry the four swing columns and share df's index.
tolerancefloat0.0005Relative fraction for the max-spread equality test (0.0005 == 0.05%). Must be >= 0 and not NaN.
min_countint2Number of consecutive same-side swings that must be equal. Must be an integer (NumPy ints accepted, bool rejected) and >= 2 — a single swing is trivially "equal" to itself and would make every confirmation an event.
sidestr'both'"both" (default), "eqh", or "eql".
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "equal_levels".

Output columns
eqhevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
eqh_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined) — all NaN on the sample data
eqlevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
eql_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined)
Raises
ValueErrorIf tolerance is negative or NaN, min_count is not an integer or is < 2, side is invalid, or the swings input fails validation.
Example

import price_action as pa
df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)

swings = pa.detect_swings(df)
result = pa.detect_equal_levels(df, swings)
result.name                         # "equal_levels"
result.metadata["repaints"]         # False
result.values[["eqh", "eql"]].sum() # events on the sample data — eqh: 0, eql: 1

detect_fvg

from price_action import detect_fvg

detect_fvg(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    min_gap_size: float = 0.0,
    direction: str = 'both',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect three-bar fair value gaps, emitted at the third bar.

At bar t (the third bar of the pattern):

  • Bullish FVG: gap low[t] - high[t-2] is strictly positive and at least min_gap_size. The unfilled zone is [high[t-2], low[t]] (fvg_lower, fvg_upper).
  • Bearish FVG: gap low[t-2] - high[t] is strictly positive and at least min_gap_size. The zone is [high[t], low[t-2]].

Both comparisons are strict on zero: candles that exactly touch (low[t] == high[t-2]) leave no gap and fire nothing. min_gap_size is in absolute price units (the same units as the dataframe's prices), and a gap exactly equal to it qualifies (>=).

On sane candles (high >= low everywhere) the two sides are mutually exclusive at a bar; if both somehow fire on malformed data, the zone columns carry the bullish side.

The event is decided from bars t-2 .. t only, so the detector is non-repainting and offset invariant, with a fixed warm-up of exactly two bars.

Relationship to the zone table. This is the per-bar view of the same geometry that detect_fvg_zones emits as a table (one frozen row per gap zone, the input to detect_fvg_mitigation). Both are built on the same private gap definition, so with join_consecutive=False the table's rows correspond one-for-one to this detector's event bars, with the same bounds. The representations differ in one way only: this detector can say "unknown" with NaN (a NaN input bar), whereas a table has no row shape for an unknown gap and simply emits nothing for such a bar. Where a NaN input matters, this per-bar surface is the one to read.

The values DataFrame shares df's index, is all float64, and its columns depend on direction:

  • "both": fvg_bullish, fvg_bearish, fvg_upper, fvg_lower;
  • "bullish" / "bearish": only that side's event column, plus fvg_upper and fvg_lower.

Event columns carry 1.0 / 0.0 / NaN; the zone columns carry the gap bounds at event bars and NaN everywhere else. The first two bars are NaN in all columns (warm-up). A NaN in a needed input — high[t-2] or low[t] for the bullish side, low[t-2] or high[t] for the bearish side — makes that side's event NaN at t; the sides are independent, so one side can be NaN while the other is decided.

Parameters

dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Only high and low are read, but the frame must satisfy the OHLC schema; volume is optional.
min_gap_sizefloat0.0Minimum gap size in absolute price units. Must be >= 0 and not NaN.
directionstr'both'"bullish", "bearish", or "both".
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "fvg".

detect_fvg_mitigation

from price_action import detect_fvg_mitigation

detect_fvg_mitigation(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    zones: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    mode: str = 'full',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Mark where price returns into each fair value gap and mitigates it.

A bullish zone [lower, upper] was left behind by price gapping up over it, so it is mitigated when price comes back down into it; a bearish zone is mitigated when price comes back up. Only the relevant extreme decides: low[t] for bullish zones, high[t] for bearish ones. mode sets how deep the return must go:

  • "touch": any entry into the zone — bullish low[t] < upper, bearish high[t] > lower. The comparison is strict, because the boundary is the gap's own edge: reaching it exactly is not yet being inside.
  • "half": reaching the midpoint (upper + lower) / 2 — bullish low[t] <= mid, bearish high[t] >= mid. This is what SMC calls consequent encroachment (the "CE" of a gap); the name here is plain geometry.
  • "full" (default): the zone is fully traversed — bullish low[t] <= lower, bearish high[t] >= upper.

The half and full comparisons are inclusive (<= / >=): the level is a depth to be reached, not an edge to be crossed.

Each zone is tracked independently and mitigates at most once (it is then consumed; later returns into the same zone fire nothing). There is no cap on how many zones a side can carry.

Activation is the bar after formation (formed_at_pos + 1): a zone's formation bar trivially touches its own boundary (a bullish zone's upper is that bar's low), and mitigation means returning. A zone whose activation bar lies at or beyond the end of df is legal and simply inert — exactly what replaying a full-data table against a shorter frame produces.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns:

  • mitigated_bullish / mitigated_bearish — 1.0 at a bar where at least one zone of that side is mitigated, 0.0 at decided bars with no mitigation, and NaN where the question is not posable: during that side's warm-up (before its earliest zone's activation bar, or throughout if the side has no zones), or where the deciding price (low for bullish, high for bearish) is NaN. A NaN bar leaves the zone state untouched — a pending mitigation is delayed, never assumed missed.
  • mitigated_bullish_level / mitigated_bearish_level — at event bars only, the threshold price that was reached (upper / midpoint / lower per mode for bullish; lower / midpoint / upper for bearish); NaN elsewhere. When several zones of one side are mitigated on the same bar the event is 1.0 and this column carries the first-formed zone's threshold (the earliest row among them, matching the retest detectors' level_pick).

modestr'full'"touch", "half", or "full" (default).
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "fvg_mitigation".

Output columns
mitigated_bullishevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
mitigated_bullish_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined)
mitigated_bearishevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
mitigated_bearish_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined)
Raises

detect_fvg_zones

from price_action import detect_fvg_zones

detect_fvg_zones(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    min_gap_size: float = 0.0,
    direction: str = 'both',
    join_consecutive: bool = False,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Emit one frozen table row per three-bar fair value gap.

The gap definition is identical to detect_fvg (the two share one private implementation of the geometry):

  • Bullish gap at bar t iff low[t] - high[t-2] is strictly positive and at least min_gap_size; the zone is [high[t-2], low[t]].
  • Bearish gap at bar t iff low[t-2] - high[t] qualifies the same way; the zone is [high[t], low[t-2]].

min_gap_size is in absolute price units and a gap exactly equal to it qualifies (>=); exactly touching candles leave no gap (strict > on zero). direction ("bullish", "bearish", "both") selects which sides are tracked at all.

A NaN in a side's needed inputs at t emits no row for that side — a table cannot carry "unknown", and inventing a row would be worse than omitting one. detect_fvg remains the NaN-aware surface: it reports NaN at exactly those bars. The sides are independent, so a bar can be unknown for one side and decided for the other.

join_consecutive=False (default). Every qualifying gap emits its own row at its own bar t. Emission depends only on bars t-2 .. t, so this mode is offset invariant as well as prefix invariant, with a fixed warm-up of two bars (metadata["warm_up_bars"] = 2, metadata["unbounded_history"] = False).

join_consecutive=True (delayed-emission merge). Gaps of the same side on consecutive bars whose zones are contiguous with the running merged zone form a run, and a run emits a single row spanning the union of its members: upper = max of members' uppers, lower = min of members' lowers. "Contiguous" means the new gap's zone overlaps or touches the running merged zone's [lower, upper] (lower_new <= upper_run and upper_new >= lower_run).

The merged row is emitted at the first bar where the run breaks — the first bar carrying no new same-side contiguous gap — and that break bar is the row's formed_at_pos. Consequences, all deliberate:

  • Every emission is delayed by at least one bar relative to join_consecutive=False, including a lone gap that never merged with anything: it is a one-member run and also emits at its break bar. The rule is uniform, with no special case for runs of length one.
  • A gap at the break bar that is not contiguous with the run being closed starts a new run immediately (and may merge with later gaps in turn), so no gap is ever lost.
  • A bar whose inputs are NaN for a side carries no gap for that side and therefore breaks that side's run (the run's row is emitted at the NaN bar). The decision is made from bars <= t and never revised.
  • A run still open at the end of the data emits nothing. Its bounds are not final — the next bar could extend it — so emitting it would break prefix invariance the moment a bar was appended. It emits later, when the run actually breaks.

Because a run has no length bound, this mode carries metadata["unbounded_history"] = True and metadata["warm_up"] = "data_dependent".

The two sides are tracked independently: on sane candles (high >= low) the sides are mutually exclusive at a bar, but opposite-side runs can interleave freely, and each side's run state is its own.

Parameters

min_gap_sizefloat0.0Minimum gap size in absolute price units. Must be >= 0 and not NaN.
directionstr'both'"bullish", "bearish", or "both" (default).
join_consecutiveboolFalseIf True, merge consecutive-bar contiguous same-side gaps into one delayed row (see above). Must be a bool.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "fvg_zones" whose values is the zone table described in the module docstring.

Output columns table — one row per object
sideobject
upperfloat64
lowerfloat64
formed_at_posint64
formed_atdatetime64[us]
Raises
TypeErrorIf join_consecutive is not a bool.
ValueErrorIf min_gap_size is negative or NaN, or direction is not one of "bullish", "bearish", "both".
Example

df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)

result = pa.detect_fvg_zones(df)
result.name                     # "fvg_zones"
result.metadata["repaints"]     # False
len(result.values)              # 155 rows — one per object on the sample data
result.values.columns.tolist()  # ['side', 'upper', 'lower', 'formed_at_pos', 'formed_at']

detect_liquidity_sweep

from price_action import detect_liquidity_sweep

detect_liquidity_sweep(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    wick_only: bool = True,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect sweeps of the liquidity resting beyond confirmed swing levels.

At each bar, swing confirmations at that bar are applied first (a fresh level is active immediately; the fractal definition guarantees a fresh swing-high level cannot be pierced upward at its own confirmation bar). Then, against the current levels:

  • Sweep high (buy-side liquidity above the last confirmed swing high): high[t] > level (strict). With wick_only=True (default) the bar must also close back below or at the level (close[t] <= level) — the wick pierced but price rejected; a bar that closes strictly above the level is a structural break, not a sweep, and consumes the level. With wick_only=False the pierce alone suffices, so a close-through bar is both a sweep and a break (the sweep fires and the level is consumed by the break part).
  • Sweep low is the mirror on low / close against the last confirmed swing-low level.

The two sides are independent; a wide bar can sweep both levels at once and emits both events. See the module docstring for the full level lifecycle (replacement while unbroken, consumption only by close-through, never by a sweep).

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns:

  • sweep_high / sweep_low — 1.0 at sweep bars, 0.0 otherwise, NaN before that side's first confirmed swing level exists and on bars whose deciding prices are NaN;
  • sweep_high_level / sweep_low_level — the swept level's price at that side's event bars, NaN elsewhere.

NaN policy (mirroring the break machine): a NaN swing event is treated as no confirmation (state preserved). The event and the consumption bookkeeping are decided separately:

  • Event: a NaN among a side's deciding prices makes that side's event NaN at the bar — with wick_only=True the deciding prices are the pierce price and the close (both are needed to decide a sweep); with wick_only=False only the pierce price decides, so a NaN close with a clean piercing high still fires the sweep.
  • Consumption: follows the close alone, unconditionally. A clean close strictly through the level consumes it even when the pierce price is NaN (the event at that bar is NaN, only the bookkeeping acts); a NaN close leaves consumption unknown, which is treated as no consumption, so the level survives the bar.
Parameters

dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe.
swingsPAResult | pd.DataFrame—The PAResult from detect_swings, or its raw values frame. Must carry the four swing columns and share df's index.
wick_onlyboolTrueIf True (default), a sweep requires the close back at or inside the level; if False, the pierce alone fires.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "liquidity_sweep".

Output columns
sweep_highevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
sweep_lowevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
sweep_high_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined)
sweep_low_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined)
Raises
TypeErrorIf wick_only is not a bool.
ValueErrorIf a required swing column is missing, the swings index does not match df's, or a confirmed swing event carries a NaN price (malformed swings frame).

df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)

swings = pa.detect_swings(df)
result = pa.detect_liquidity_sweep(df, swings)
result.name                         # "liquidity_sweep"
