from price_action import detect_ob_mitigation

detect_ob_mitigation(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    zones: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    mode: str = 'full',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Mark where price returns into each order block and mitigates it.

A bullish order block sits below the upward break that identified it, so it is mitigated when price comes back down into it; a bearish block sits above its downward break and is mitigated when price comes back up. Only the relevant extreme decides: low[t] for bullish zones, high[t] for bearish ones. mode sets how deep the return must go:

  • "touch": any entry into the zone — bullish low[t] < upper, bearish high[t] > lower. The comparison is strict: reaching the zone's own edge exactly is not yet being inside it.
  • "half": reaching the midpoint (upper + lower) / 2 — bullish low[t] <= mid, bearish high[t] >= mid. (The SMC literature usually calls this the block's "50% level" or "mean threshold"; the name here is plain geometry.)
  • "full" (default): the zone is fully traversed — bullish low[t] <= lower, bearish high[t] >= upper.

The half and full comparisons are inclusive (<= / >=): the level is a depth to be reached, not an edge to be crossed.

Each zone is tracked independently and mitigates at most once (it is then consumed; later returns into the same zone fire nothing). There is no cap on how many zones a side can carry.

Activation is the bar after formation (formed_at_pos + 1, the break bar + 1 — see the module docstring). A zone whose activation bar lies at or beyond the end of df is legal and simply inert — exactly what replaying a full-data table against a shorter frame produces.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns:

  • ob_mitigated_bullish / ob_mitigated_bearish — 1.0 at a bar where at least one zone of that side is mitigated, 0.0 at decided bars with no mitigation, and NaN where the question is not posable: during that side's warm-up (before its earliest zone's activation bar, or throughout if the side has no zones), or where the deciding price (low for bullish, high for bearish) is NaN. A NaN bar leaves the zone state untouched — a pending mitigation is delayed, never assumed missed.
  • ob_mitigated_bullish_level / ob_mitigated_bearish_level — at event bars only, the threshold price that was reached (upper / midpoint / lower per mode for bullish; lower / midpoint / upper for bearish); NaN elsewhere. When several zones of one side are mitigated on the same bar the event is 1.0 and this column carries the first-formed zone's threshold (the earliest row among them, matching the retest detectors' level_pick).

Columns beyond the four the machine reads are tolerated, so an order-block table's ob_pos / strength (and a breaker table's origin_pos) pass through untouched.

detect_order_block_zones

from price_action import detect_order_block_zones

detect_order_block_zones(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    require_bos: bool = True,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    zone: str = 'range',
    volume_window: int | None = 20,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Emit one frozen table row per order block, with a volume-strength column.

The order-block definition is identical to detect_order_blocks (the two share one private implementation): a bullish order block is the last decisive down-close candle (close < open) before an upward structural break, a bearish one the last up-close candle before a downward break, found by an unbounded backward scan from the break bar that skips dojis and same-direction candles. require_bos, break_mode and zone mean exactly what they mean there, and the anchoring breaks come from the same shared BOS/CHoCH machine. Order blocks are defined many ways across the SMC literature; this is the one "last_opposite_candle" method, recorded in metadata["method"].

A row is emitted at exactly the bars where that detector emits a 1.0, with the same bounds — except that a bar whose event is NaN (unknown), or whose bounds are unusable (NaN, or degenerate with upper <= lower), emits no row; see the module docstring for why. Every emitted row therefore carries two finite bounds with upper > lower, which is what the downstream zone machines require.

The row's formed_at_pos is the break bar, not the order-block candle (which is carried separately as ob_pos): the break is what makes the zone knowable, so it is the formation bar for every lifecycle purpose — including the formed_at_pos + 1 activation used by detect_ob_mitigation and detect_breaker_blocks. A bar that breaks both sides (a wide bar in wick mode) emits up to two rows, the bullish one first.

strength divides the order-block candle's volume by the simple mean of volume over the volume_window bars ending at that candle (inclusive, so the candle's own volume is part of its own average and a value of 1.0 means "exactly average"). Details, all deliberate:

  • the window is truncated at the start of history: an order-block candle at position p averages over max(0, p - volume_window + 1) .. p, which is fewer bars near the start rather than no value at all;
  • NaN volumes inside the window are excluded from the mean (they are missing data, not zeros), but a NaN volume on the order-block candle itself makes its strength NaN — there is nothing to compare;
  • a window whose mean works out to 0.0 yields NaN rather than an infinity;
  • volume is assumed non-negative, as traded volume is: a frame carrying negative volumes still produces finite ratios, but meaningless ones;
  • volume_window=None switches the metric off entirely: strength is all-NaN and the volume column is not required at all, so a volume-less frame is fine.

strength is a descriptive feature for research, not a signal: no claim is made that a high-volume order block behaves differently from a low-volume one.

Parameters

require_bosboolTrueIf True (default) only BOS breaks anchor order blocks; if False CHoCH breaks anchor them too.
break_modestr'close'"close" or "wick" — passed to the break machine.
zonestr'range'"range" (candle low/high, default) or "body" (candle open/close).
volume_windowint | None20Number of bars (>= 1) the strength average spans, or None to disable the metric and the volume requirement.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "ob_zones" whose values is the zone table described in the module docstring.

Output columns table — one row per object

lowerfloat64
ob_posint64
formed_at_posint64
formed_atdatetime64[us]
strengthfloat64

ValueErrorIf volume_window is neither None nor an integer >= 1, zone or break_mode is invalid, a required swing column is missing, the swings index does not match df's, or a confirmed swing event carries a NaN price (malformed swings frame).

df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)

result = pa.detect_order_block_zones(df, swings)

detect_order_blocks

from price_action import detect_order_blocks

detect_order_blocks(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    require_bos: bool = True,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    zone: str = 'range',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect order blocks by the last_opposite_candle method.

A bullish order block is the last decisive down-close candle (close < open) before an upward structural break; a bearish order block the last decisive up-close candle (close > open) before a downward break. The event is emitted at the break bar t and the zone columns describe the earlier order-block candle — everything is known at t, so the detector is non-repainting (see the module docstring). Order blocks are defined many ways across the SMC literature; this is the last_opposite_candle method, and the result makes no claim about predictive value.

The anchoring breaks are produced by the shared BOS/CHoCH break machine (the same one behind detect_bos / detect_choch). With require_bos=True (default) only BOS breaks anchor order blocks; with require_bos=False CHoCH breaks anchor them too. break_mode is passed straight through to that machine.

From the break bar the detector scans strictly earlier bars for the most recent opposite candle, skipping dojis and same-direction candles. The scan is unbounded (all bars < t); exhausting history without an opposite candle yields 0.0 (a qualifying break with no order block), and meeting a NaN open/close before any decisive candle yields NaN (the order block is unknowable).

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has six float64 columns:

  • ob_bullish / ob_bearish — 1.0 at a break bar whose backward scan found an order block, 0.0 at bars with no qualifying event (including qualifying breaks whose scan found nothing), and NaN where the anchoring break event itself is NaN (inherited from the machine: that side's data-dependent warm-up before its first swing level, or a NaN deciding price) or where the scan hit a NaN open/close before a decisive candle;
  • ob_bullish_upper / ob_bullish_lower (and the bearish mirror) — the order-block candle's zone at event bars, NaN elsewhere. With zone="range" (default) the bounds are the candle's [low, high]; with zone="body" they are [min(open, close), max(open, close)].

The two sides are independent: a bar that breaks both levels (a wide bar in wick mode) runs both scans and can fire both order blocks with their own zones. With zone="range", if the order-block candle's high or low is NaN while its open/close were decisive, the event is still 1.0 and only the missing zone bound is NaN.

Parameters

dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe.
swingsPAResult | pd.DataFrame—The PAResult from detect_swings, or its raw values frame. Must carry the four swing columns and share df's index.
require_bosboolTrueIf True (default) only BOS breaks anchor order blocks; if False CHoCH breaks anchor them too.

detect_ote

from price_action import detect_ote

detect_ote(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    retracement: Sequence[float] = (0.618, 0.79),
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Publish the retracement band of the most recent impulse leg per bar.

The leg. The detector tracks the last confirmed swing high H and the last confirmed swing low L (price and confirmation bar). Once both exist, the order of their confirmations names the leg: if L confirmed before H the market last travelled upward, so the impulse is up and the bullish band is active; if H confirmed before L the impulse is down and the bearish band is active. Exactly one direction is active at a time — confirming a swing high always makes the leg bullish, confirming a swing low always makes it bearish.

Same-bar confirmation ties. Both sides can confirm at one bar (an outside bar can complete a fractal high and a fractal low at once), which leaves the confirmation order undefined. The tie is broken by that bar's own close direction — the move that ended the bar is the one that came last: close > open -> bullish leg, close < open -> bearish leg. A NaN open or close makes the tie equally undecidable and is handled identically to an exact doji (close == open), which carries no evidence either way. This mirrors the close-direction tie-break detect_swings_zigzag uses for its both-threshold bar, recorded as metadata["tie_break"] = "close_direction".

An undecidable tie inherits whatever direction was last set (metadata["tie_break_fallback"] = "keep_previous") — not merely the direction of a previously published band. A lone one-sided confirmation already sets the direction even though no band could be drawn yet (the other side had never confirmed), so a doji tie after a lone swing high publishes a bullish band at the tie bar: the tie supplies the missing level, the inherited direction says which way to read the leg. The bar stays in warm-up only when no confirmation has ever occurred, leaving nothing to inherit. The levels themselves are always updated at a tie bar; only the direction is ever in question.

The band. With leg range R = H_price - L_price and retracement = (r1, r2):

  • bullish (retracing down from the leg's high)::
upper = H_price - r1 * R
lower = H_price - r2 * R
  • bearish (retracing up from the leg's low, the exact mirror — the down leg spans the same two prices, so its range is the same R = H_price - L_price)::
lower = L_price + r1 * R
upper = L_price + r2 * R

Since r1 < r2, lower < upper in both cases and the band's width is (r2 - r1) * R. With the default depths the bullish band covers the 61.8% to 79% retracement of the up leg and the bearish band the same depths of the down leg.

The band is recomputed only at swing confirmations; between them it is frozen and only the close moves against it.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has six float64 columns, following the state-series convention of detect_range rather than the event-bar convention:

  • ote_bullish — 1.0 iff the bullish leg is active and lower <= close[t] <= upper (both edges inclusive: a close exactly on a retracement level is in the band, recorded as metadata["band_edges"] = "inclusive"), 0.0 iff the bullish leg is active and the close is outside the band, NaN otherwise;
  • ote_bullish_upper / ote_bullish_lower — the standing band on every bar the bullish leg is active, including bars where ote_bullish is 0.0 (price away from the band does not un-draw it) and bars whose close is NaN; NaN only where the bullish leg is not active at all;
  • ote_bearish, ote_bearish_upper, ote_bearish_lower — the mirror, filled exactly when the bearish leg is active.

All six columns are NaN when there is no usable leg, namely during warm-up (a side has never confirmed, or the only confirmation ever was an undecidable same-bar tie, which leaves no direction to inherit) and on a degenerate leg (R <= 0, i.e. the last confirmed swing low sits at or above the last confirmed swing high — reachable in choppy structure, where the band would be empty or inverted). The inactive direction's three columns are always NaN; ote_bullish / ote_bearish is additionally NaN on an active leg whose close[t] is NaN (membership unknown) while its two band columns stay filled.

NaN swing events. A NaN in swing_high / swing_low is treated as no confirmation (metadata["nan_swing_policy"] = "treated_as_no_swing"): the leg and the band are left exactly as they were, so the standing band survives the bar and keeps being evaluated.

Parameters

retracementSequence[float](0.618, 0.79)The (r1, r2) retracement depths as fractions of the leg range, shallow first. Must be a 2-element tuple/list of floats with 0 < r1 < r2 < 1 and no NaN.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "ote".

Output columns

ote_bullish_upperlevel / position (NaN except where defined)
ote_bullish_lowerlevel / position (NaN except where defined)
ote_bearishevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)

detect_premium_discount

from price_action import detect_premium_discount

detect_premium_discount(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Measure where each bar's close sits inside the active dealing range.

Walking the bars in order, the detector keeps the price of the last confirmed swing high (high_level) and the last confirmed swing low (low_level). Both are replaced as soon as a fresh same-side pivot confirms — the confirmation is applied at its own bar, so the new level is already in force there and the reported fraction moves at exactly that bar. With both levels in hand the bar's position in the range is:

range_position = (close[t] - low_level) / (high_level - low_level)

so 0.0 is the range low, 1.0 the range high and 0.5 equilibrium.

The position is not clamped. A close that runs beyond the range prints > 1.0 (above the last confirmed high) or < 0.0 (below the last confirmed low), which is the common case right after a structural break — the level that was just taken has not been replaced yet. Clamping would destroy exactly that information, so range_position is a position measure with an unbounded codomain rather than a percentage.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has three float64 columns:

  • range_position — the fraction above, NaN when the range is not measurable (see below);
  • premium — 1.0 iff range_position > 0.5 strictly, else 0.0;
  • discount — 1.0 iff range_position < 0.5 strictly, else 0.0.

A close landing exactly at equilibrium is therefore neither premium nor discount: both flags are 0.0. That is deliberate — the two flags describe the two open half-boxes, and assigning the midpoint to one of them would be an arbitrary tie-break. A consumer that wants a partition can test discount == 0.0 instead.

All three columns are NaN at the same bars, namely when:

  • warm-up — one or both sides have never confirmed, so the box has no edge (data-dependent length; once both edges exist the columns never return to the warm-up NaN);
  • the range is degenerate or inverted (high_level <= low_level). This is reachable in choppy structure: the last confirmed swing low can sit above the last confirmed swing high (e.g. a low confirming after a sharp rally that has not yet printed a new pivot high). The denominator would be zero or negative, turning the fraction into a division by zero or a silently mirrored measure, so the bar is reported as unmeasurable instead;
  • close[t] is NaN (the position is unknown at that bar).

NaN swing events. A NaN in swing_high / swing_low is treated as no confirmation (metadata["nan_swing_policy"] = "treated_as_no_swing"): the level is simply not updated and the previous one stays in force, so the state survives the bar and the columns still carry the (older) measurable range there.

columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "premium_discount".

Output columns
range_positionlevel / position (NaN except where defined)
premiumevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
discountevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
Raises

patterns

Classic chart patterns — double tops/bottoms, head & shoulders, ranges · 5 functions

Chart patterns are the oldest layer of technical analysis — Edwards and Magee catalogued double tops, head-and-shoulders and rectangles in 1948 — and also its least reproducible: two chartists rarely agree on whether a pattern counts, how equal two peaks must be, or where the neckline sits. This module's answer is to make each pattern a strict geometric predicate over confirmed swings, from either swing engine, with every tolerance a parameter recorded in metadata and the definition named in metadata["method"].

equal(a, b) ⇔ |a − b| ≤ tol · max(|a|, |b|)   — relative price equality; tol = 0.002 for double tops/bottoms
double top ⇔ consecutive swing highs H₁, H₂ with equal(H₁, H₂) and ≥ 1 swing low between   — fires at the first close below the lowest such low
H&S ⇔ consecutive swing highs L, H, R with H > L and H > R, a swing low in each gap   — fires at the first close below the lowest gap low
range ⇔ last n swing highs and last n swing lows each with max − min ≤ tol · max(|max|, |min|)   — n = min_swings = 2, tol = 0.005

All four reversal detectors fire at the neckline break (metadata["anchor"] = "neckline_break"), not at the second peak or the third shoulder. A candidate arms at the confirmation bar of its last swing, and its neckline is frozen there; the pattern completes at the first bar from then on whose close (or wick, with break_mode="wick") lies strictly beyond it. That bar can be the arming bar itself, even when price had already crossed the neckline before the candidate armed: the test is a level comparison, not a crossing. Any newer swing of the pattern's side replaces an armed candidate — before that bar's break decision — and an unbroken candidate simply never fires. "Between" is measured on confirmation bars, so a swing confirming on the same bar as a peak counts for no pair. Double tops and bottoms take tolerance for the peak equality; head-and-shoulders imposes no shoulder equality unless shoulder_tolerance is given, and draws a horizontal neckline at the lower of the two gap troughs (the higher gap peak for the inverse), a deliberately conservative choice where classical charting often draws a sloped one. The event column comes with a *_level column — the higher peak, the lower trough, or the head — and a *_neckline column, both filled at the event bar only.

detect_range is the exception in kind: a per-bar state series. A range forms when the last min_swings swing highs cluster within the max-spread tolerance and the last min_swings swing lows do too, with the highest of those highs above the lowest of those lows; the band is frozen at those two extremes. range_active is 1.0 on every bar inside it, with range_upper / range_lower filled on all of them, until the first close strictly outside the band (a wick beyond it, in wick mode). The exit test already runs on the formation bar, so a band that is breached as it forms never activates. While a range is active new swings are ignored; after an exit only swings confirmed later can form the next one.

All five detectors are causal state machines with unbounded history: prefix invariant, not offset invariant, and NaN until the question can first be posed — the first armed candidate, or min_swings swings on each side. A NaN deciding price while a candidate is armed gives a NaN event and keeps the candidate armed. At their defaults these strict definitions fire rarely: on the 500-bar sample with default fractal swings, only the head-and-shoulders top fires (three times), and the double top, double bottom, inverse head-and-shoulders and range produce no event. The detectors describe a completed shape; they make no claim about what follows it.

When to reach for this module: classical patterns as reproducible events — neckline-confirmed reversals and a consolidation-state mask with its live bounds, with the folklore replaced by parameters.

from price_action import detect_double_bottom

detect_double_bottom(
    df: pd.DataFrame,

Detect double bottoms, emitted at the neckline break (mirror of the top).

The exact mirror of detect_double_top: a candidate forms from two consecutive confirmed swing lows equal within tolerance with at least one confirmed swing high strictly between them; the neckline is the highest such swing high. Completion is the first bar at or after arming whose deciding price rises strictly above the neckline (close[t] > neckline in close mode, high[t] > neckline in wick mode).

The double_bottom event fires 1.0 at the break, double_bottom_level carries the lower of the two troughs (conservative support) and double_bottom_neckline the neckline; both are filled only at event bars. Lifecycle, warm-up, and NaN handling are identical to the double top.

detect_double_top

from price_action import detect_double_top

detect_double_top(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    tolerance: float = 0.002,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect double tops, emitted at the neckline break.

A double-top candidate forms from two consecutive confirmed swing highs (no other swing high between them) whose prices are equal within the relative tolerance (see _prices_equal), provided at least one confirmed swing low sits strictly between them. "Strictly between" is measured on confirmation bars: a swing low whose confirmation bar coincides with either peak's confirmation bar is between no pair at all — it counts neither toward the pair it shares a bar with nor toward the next one. The neckline is the lowest qualifying swing low. The candidate becomes armed at the second peak's confirmation bar, and the neckline is frozen there — a swing low confirming later, while the candidate is armed, does not move it.

The pattern completes at the first bar t at or after the arming bar whose deciding price falls strictly below the neckline: close[t] < neckline with break_mode="close" (default) or low[t] < neckline with break_mode="wick". The event double_top fires 1.0 there, double_top_level carries the higher of the two peaks (the conservative resistance) and double_top_neckline the neckline price; both level columns are filled only at event bars.

Lifecycle. While a candidate is armed, any new confirmed swing high replaces it — the two peaks are no longer the most recent consecutive pair, so the machine re-evaluates the new last-two-highs pair (which may arm a fresh candidate or leave none). Replacement happens before the bar's break decision: when a new swing high confirms on the very bar that would have broken the old candidate's neckline, the replacement wins and the break is evaluated against the new candidate (or none), never the old one. If the neckline break never comes the candidate simply never fires. After a completion the candidate is consumed and the machine keeps walking; the completed pattern's second peak remains the most recent swing high, so it can serve as the first peak of the next candidate.

Warm-up and NaN. The double_top column is NaN until the first candidate ever arms (the question is not posed before then) and 0.0 on non-event bars afterwards. A NaN deciding price while a candidate is armed yields a NaN event at that bar and leaves the candidate armed.

break_modestr'close'"close" (default) or "wick".
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.

detect_head_and_shoulders

from price_action import detect_head_and_shoulders

detect_head_and_shoulders(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    shoulder_tolerance: float | None = None,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect head-and-shoulders tops, emitted at the neckline break.

A candidate forms from three consecutive confirmed swing highs L, H, R (no other swing high interleaved) with the head H strictly above both shoulders L and R, provided at least one confirmed swing low sits strictly between L and H and at least one strictly between H and R. "Strictly between" is measured on confirmation bars: a swing low whose confirmation bar coincides with any triple member's confirmation bar sits inside no gap (it counts toward no triple at all). The neckline is the horizontal at the lower of the two gap troughs — the lowest swing low across both gaps — a deliberately conservative choice. When shoulder_tolerance is not None the shoulders L and R must additionally be equal within that relative fraction; None (default) imposes no shoulder-equality constraint. The candidate arms at R's confirmation bar.

Completion is the first bar at or after arming whose deciding price falls strictly below the neckline (close in close mode, low in wick mode). head_and_shoulders fires 1.0 there, head_and_shoulders_level carries the head price H and head_and_shoulders_neckline the neckline; both are filled only at event bars.

Lifecycle mirrors the double top: any new confirmed swing high re-evaluates the last-three-highs triple (replacing any armed candidate) before the bar's break decision — a swing high confirming on the would-be break bar means the break is evaluated against the re-evaluated candidate, never the old one — a completion consumes the candidate, and the event column is NaN until the first candidate arms. A NaN deciding price while armed yields NaN and leaves the candidate armed. After a completion the machine keeps walking, and the consumed pattern's later peaks remain in the sliding window, so they can participate in the next triple.

detect_range

from price_action import detect_range

detect_range(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    tolerance: float = 0.005,
    min_swings: int = 2,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect horizontal consolidation ranges as a per-bar state series.

Formation. Walking confirmed swings, a range forms at the first bar where the last min_swings consecutive swing highs are all within tolerance of one another and the last min_swings consecutive swing lows are all within tolerance of one another. "Within tolerance" is measured by max spread per side: a side qualifies iff (max - min) <= tolerance * max(abs(max), abs(min)) over its min_swings prices (tolerance a relative fraction). The band bounds are frozen at formation: range_upper is the maximum of the qualifying highs, range_lower the minimum of the qualifying lows. A degenerate band (range_upper <= range_lower) does not form.

Active life. From the formation bar (inclusive) the range stays active until the first bar whose deciding price exits [range_lower, range_upper] strictly: close outside in close mode (default), or high > range_upper / low < range_lower in wick mode. The exit test runs on the formation bar itself: if that bar's deciding price is already strictly outside the just-frozen bounds (common in wick mode, where the confirming bar's wick can overshoot the band), the range never activates — range_active is 0.0 there and the qualifying windows are cleared. If the formation bar's deciding price is NaN, formation is undecidable and is conservatively treated like an exit for state purposes: the bar emits NaN, the range does not activate, and the windows are cleared. An exit bar is already outside, so range_active is 0.0 there (not 1.0), and the machine then looks for a fresh range using only swings confirmed after the exit — the qualifying window is reset, which is simpler and cleaner than reusing pre-exit swings. While a range is active, swing confirmations are ignored regardless of their price: the bounds stay frozen until the range deactivates.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has three float64 columns:

  • range_active — 1.0 on active bars (formation bar included), 0.0 otherwise, NaN during warm-up (until min_swings swings per side have confirmed at least once, so the formation question is posable), NaN on a bar whose deciding price is NaN while a range is active (state preserved), and NaN on a would-be formation bar whose deciding price is NaN (formation abandoned, windows cleared);
  • range_upper / range_lower — the frozen band bounds on every bar the range is in force (active bars, including NaN-decider bars), NaN elsewhere.
Parameters

tolerancefloat0.005Relative fraction for the per-side spread (0.005 == 0.5%). Must be >= 0 and not NaN.
min_swingsint2Number of consecutive swings per side that must cluster. Must be an integer — any numbers.Integral (NumPy ints included) except bool; floats (NaN included) are rejected — and >= 2.
break_modestr'close'"close" (default) or "wick".
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.

levels

Horizontal support/resistance — level table, breakouts, retests · 3 functions

Horizontal support and resistance is the observation that markets remember prices: a level where price reversed before attracts orders when it is revisited. This module makes the idea measurable in two stages. First, detect_support_resistance clusters confirmed swing pivots — swing lows into support, swing highs into resistance — and emits a level table: one row per level (side, price, formation bar, touch count), frozen at the bar where it forms and never revised.

The clustering is causal and greedy. Per side the detector keeps a set of open clusters, each anchored at its first member's price. At every swing confirmation the new pivot joins the open cluster whose anchor is within tolerance and nearest to it — ties go to the oldest cluster — or opens a fresh cluster of its own. A cluster that reaches min_touches (default 2) members forms a level at that confirmation bar: level_price is the mean of the member pivots, touches records the count at formation (always min_touches, not a running count), and the cluster closes. Later nearby pivots start new clusters, so near-duplicate levels can accumulate over time; touches of an existing level are not counted.

level = mean of min_touches same-side pivots, each within tolerance of the cluster's first pivot
relative: |p − a| ≤ tolerance · max(|p|, |a|); atr: |p − a| ≤ tolerance · ATR[t] — ATR: simple mean of the gap-aware true range over atr_window bars ending at the confirmation bar t
breakout ⇔ first close (or wick) strictly beyond level_price at t ≥ formed_at_pos — retest: first later bar whose [low, high] overlaps level_price · (1 ± retest_tolerance)

Two units for "the same price". With tolerance_mode="relative" (default) tolerance is a fraction of price (0.002 = 0.2%), so the band scales with the price level. With tolerance_mode="atr" it is a multiple of recent volatility: the simple mean of the gap-aware true range over atr_window (default 14) bars ending at the confirmation bar where the join is decided, truncated at the start of history and with NaN true ranges excluded — the more portable unit when one parameter set runs across instruments or regimes. Wilder's recursive smoothing is deliberately not used, since its seeded accumulator would make the same bar's value depend on where the frame starts. Each join reads the ATR known at its own bar, so members of one cluster may have been admitted under different ATR values, and an ATR that cannot be computed (every true range in its window NaN) makes the join undecidable: the pivot opens a fresh cluster. The 0.002 default is a relative-mode number — read as an ATR multiple it is near-exact equality — so ATR mode wants a tolerance of its own (0.5 is "within half an ATR"). Only the equality test changes; anchors, nearest match, the oldest-cluster tie-break and formation are identical in both modes.

The second stage is the level-interaction machine, shared by detect_level_breakout and detect_level_retest so their geometry is identical by construction. Every level in the table is tracked at once, from its formation bar inclusive — unlike the zone lifecycles, a level can break on the bar where it forms. A resistance breaks up at the first bar whose close (break_mode="close", default) or high ("wick") is strictly above level_price, a support breaks down on the mirror test, levels are only tested in their natural direction, and each breaks at most once. A retest is the first bar strictly after the break whose range overlaps the band level_price · (1 ± retest_tolerance) (default 0.002, a relative fraction in either tolerance mode); each broken level retests at most once. When several levels break on one bar the level column carries the furthest (the highest up, the lowest down); when several retest, the first-formed. A NaN deciding price delays a break or retest and never cancels it, and each direction stays NaN until its first level of that side has formed.

The table is append-only: computed on a prefix df.iloc[:k] (with swings recomputed for that prefix) it is an exact row-prefix of the full-data table. Nothing expires — a level stays live until price breaks it, and a broken level waits for its retest just as long — so a level formed thousands of bars ago can still fire, and the breakout and retest detectors carry unbounded_history = True: truncation invariant, not offset invariant.

When to reach for this module: the horizontal memory of the chart — a frozen, auditable table of swing-clustered levels, measured in price or volatility units, plus non-repainting breakout and retest events against it.

detect_level_breakout

from price_action import detect_level_breakout

detect_level_breakout(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    levels: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect the first breakout of each level in a support / resistance table.

A resistance level breaks up at the first bar t at or after its formed_at_pos whose deciding price is strictly greater than its level_price — the bar close in break_mode="close" (default) or the bar high in break_mode="wick". A support level breaks down with the close / low strictly below. A level is active on its formation bar (inclusive), so a break on that very bar fires. Such formation-bar self-breaks are not rare in wick mode — the confirming bar's wick often overshoots a fresh level (roughly 1.5--4.7% of levels on random walks, rising with the clustering tolerance, versus ~0.1--0.5% in close mode) — which is worth knowing when choosing break_mode. Each level breaks at most once; a later cross of an already-broken level fires nothing. Levels are only tested in their natural direction, so a resistance never breaks downward and a support never upward.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns:

  • breakout_up / breakout_down — 1.0 at a bar where at least one resistance (support) level breaks, 0.0 at bars with no such break, and NaN during that direction's warm-up (before the first resistance / support level's formed_at_pos, or throughout if that side has no levels) or where the deciding price is NaN (the level state is left unchanged — it keeps waiting);
  • breakout_up_level / breakout_down_level — at event bars only, the furthest level broken that bar (max level_price up, min down); NaN elsewhere.

detect_level_retest

from price_action import detect_level_retest

detect_level_retest(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    levels: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    retest_tolerance: float = 0.002,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect the first retest of each broken level in a level table.

A level's breakout is found first (by the same rule and break_mode as detect_level_breakout). Its retest is then the first bar t strictly after the breakout bar whose range overlaps the level's tolerance band [level_price*(1-retest_tolerance), level_price*(1+retest_tolerance)] — that is, low[t] <= band_upper and high[t] >= band_lower. A touch on the breakout bar itself does not count. Each level retests at most once. With retest_tolerance=0 the band collapses to the level and an exact touch (low[t] <= level_price <= high[t]) is required. Prices are assumed positive for the band definition; for a negative level_price the two bounds invert arithmetically (not special-cased).

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns:

  • retest_up / retest_down — 1.0 at a bar where at least one up-broken resistance (down-broken support) level is retested, 0.0 at bars with no such retest, and NaN during that direction's warm-up (mirroring the breakout warm-up: before the first resistance / support level's formed_at_pos, or throughout if that side has no levels) or where the deciding high / low is NaN (level state unchanged);
  • retest_up_level / retest_down_level — at event bars only, the first-formed level among those retested that bar (the earliest table row); NaN elsewhere.

Because breakouts are computed internally, NaN deciding-price bars only delay a breakout (and hence its retest) rather than cancelling it.

detect_support_resistance

from price_action import detect_support_resistance

detect_support_resistance(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    tolerance: float = 0.002,
    min_touches: int = 2,
    side: str = 'both',
    tolerance_mode: str = 'relative',
    atr_window: int = 14,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect horizontal support / resistance levels by clustering swing pivots.

Walking the bars in order, the detector clusters confirmed swing pivots by price. Resistance levels cluster swing-high pivot prices; support levels cluster swing-low pivot prices. side selects which are computed ("support", "resistance", or "both").

Causal greedy clustering. Per side the detector maintains a set of open clusters. At each swing confirmation with pivot price p it looks for open same-side clusters whose anchor (the first member's price) is within tolerance of p. Among the matches it joins the cluster with the nearest anchor; ties are broken toward the oldest cluster (deterministic). If nothing matches, p opens a new cluster anchored at itself.

What "within tolerance" means is set by tolerance_mode:

  • "relative" (default): abs(p - a) <= tolerance * max(abs(p), abs(a)) — the same relative-fraction test the pattern detectors use.
  • "atr": abs(p - a) <= tolerance * ATR[t], so tolerance is read as an ATR multiple (0.5 == "within half an ATR") and the band adapts to volatility rather than to price level. ATR is the simple-mean true range over atr_window bars defined in price_action.levels._atr (metadata["atr_method"] = "sma_true_range"), and t is the confirmation bar at which the join decision is made — the ATR known when the pivot confirms, never a later one. One consequence worth naming: the admissible distance is re-read at every confirmation, so members of the same cluster may have been admitted under different ATR values (a pivot that would not join today might have joined in a more volatile stretch). That is deliberate; the decision at each bar reads only bars <= t, so the result stays deterministic and prefix invariant, which is the property that matters. When ATR[t] is NaN (every true range in the window is NaN) the join question is undecidable; since a table has no way to express "unknown", the conservative reading is taken — no match, so the pivot opens a fresh cluster.

Formation. When a cluster reaches min_touches members a level forms at that confirmation bar: level_price is the mean of the member pivot prices (frozen), formed_at_pos is the bar's position, and touches is min_touches. The cluster then closes (is removed); later nearby pivots start fresh clusters, so several near-duplicate levels can accumulate over time — accepted MVP behaviour. Later touches of an already-formed level are deliberately not tracked in v0.1.

A NaN swing event is treated as no confirmation and never joins or opens a cluster (metadata["nan_swing_policy"] = "treated_as_no_swing").

When "both", a bar carrying both a swing-high and a swing-low confirmation can form a resistance and a support level on the same bar; the resistance row is emitted first (deterministic ordering).

Parameters

min_touchesint2Number of pivots a cluster must gather to form a level. Must be an integer (NumPy ints accepted, bool rejected) and >= 2.
sidestr'both'"support", "resistance", or "both" (default).
tolerance_modestr'relative'"relative" (default) or "atr" — how tolerance is interpreted, as described above.

Returns

trendlines

Diagonal support/resistance — trendline table, breakouts, retests · 3 functions

A trendline is support or resistance with a slope: the line a trending market keeps respecting. Chartists draw them by eye; this module draws them by rule. detect_trendlines pairs consecutive same-side confirmed swing pivots: a new swing low strictly above the previous swing low draws an ascending support line, a new swing high strictly below the previous swing high a descending resistance line, and equal prices draw nothing while the new pivot still becomes the reference for the next comparison. Every qualifying pair emits a row, so three rising lows yield two support rows sharing the middle pivot. Each row is frozen into a trendline table at the bar where its second anchor confirms — the diagonal analogue of the level table. Anchor positions are pivot bar positions: confirmation_bar − right for fractal swings, or read straight from the swing_high_pos / swing_low_pos columns that detect_swings_zigzag publishes (metadata["position_source"]).

Two geometries, one trigger. method decides how the line is drawn and nothing else — which rows are emitted, and when, is identical. "pivot_pair" (default) is the straight line through the two pivots. "fit" fits a line to every bar of the window [anchor1_pos .. formed_at_pos] — lows for support, highs for resistance — under the hard constraint that it never crosses price there. The fit is solved in closed form: the intercept is pinned to the window's extremum (the earliest bar on a tie), which turns the constraint into a feasible slope interval that always contains zero and the squared-error objective into a convex parabola, so the optimum is the anchored least-squares slope clamped into that interval — exact, with no iteration and no tolerance. The anchor prices then become the fitted line's values at the two anchor positions. Because the pair only gates emission, a fitted support line may come out flat or even negative, and it is reported as fitted. NaN bars are excluded from the fit; a window with no usable price keeps the two-point line, and one with a single usable price gets the flat line through it.

pivot_pair: slope = (P₂ − P₁) / (p₂ − p₁) — the two anchors' prices and bar positions
fit: slope = clamp(Σ dx·dp / Σ dx², L, U) — offsets from the window's extremum; [L, U] = the slopes that keep the line from crossing price
projected level at t = anchor2_price + slope · (t − anchor2_pos) — the line extends forward in time

Quality columns. Every row, under either method, carries a quality triple measured over the line's own window with the same projection the breakout/retest machine uses, and frozen at formation: touches counts the bars whose low (support) or high (resistance) lies on the line within the relative touch_tolerance (default 0.001); score is the mean relative distance from the line, lower meaning the line hugs price more tightly; body_cross is 1.0 when the line passes strictly through some candle body in the window. The columns are reported, never used to filter rows, and are not machine inputs — a table without them drives the breakout and retest detectors unchanged. A fitted line sits at or below every usable low (support) or at or above every usable high (resistance) of its window, so on OHLC-consistent candles with no missing low or high it cannot pass strictly through a body, up to floating-point rounding (a bar whose low or high is NaN is excluded from the fit, and the line may cross that bar's body); body_cross chiefly separates pivot-pair lines that cut through price from those that do not.

Because a trendline's level moves with every bar, its interaction events are projections, and the trendline-interaction machine shared by detect_trendline_breakout and detect_trendline_retest keeps one active line per side: the most recently formed one, active from its formed_at_pos inclusive. A newly formed line replaces the side's unbroken active line, and the replaced line is dropped — it never breaks and never retests. Resistance breaks up at the first bar whose close (or high, by break_mode) is strictly above its projection, support breaks down on the mirror test, a break on the formation bar itself can fire, and a broken line is consumed: the side has no active line until the next one forms. Every line that broke then waits independently for a retest — the first bar strictly after its break whose range overlaps the band line(t) · (1 ± retest_tolerance), with the line projected to the retest bar, so the band drifts with the slope. The level columns record the projected value at the event bar (the first-formed line when several retest at once), keeping every event auditable against its table row.

The table is append-only and row-prefix invariant: computed on a prefix of the data, with swings recomputed for it, it is an exact row-prefix of the full-data table. Broken lines accumulate as retest candidates without a cap, so the event detectors carry unbounded_history = True — truncation invariant, not offset invariant.

When to reach for this module: the diagonal memory of the chart — an auditable table of swing-anchored trendlines, drawn through two pivots or fitted to the whole span, with quality columns to filter on, plus non-repainting breakout and retest events against their projected levels.

detect_trendline_breakoutdetect_trendline_retestdetect_trendlines

detect_trendline_breakout

from price_action import detect_trendline_breakout

detect_trendline_breakout(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    trendlines: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect the first breakout of each side's active trendline.

Per side the machine tracks a single active line — the most recently formed one, which replaces any earlier unbroken line. A resistance line breaks up at the first bar at or after its formed_at_pos whose deciding price is strictly greater than the line projected to that bar — the bar close in break_mode="close" (default) or the bar high in break_mode="wick". A support line breaks down with the close / low strictly below its projection. A line is active on its formation bar (inclusive), so a same-bar formation+break can fire. Each line breaks at most once and is then consumed; the side has no active line until a later row forms.

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns:

  • breakout_up / breakout_down — 1.0 at a bar where the active resistance (support) line breaks, 0.0 at bars with no break, and NaN during that direction's warm-up (before the first resistance / support line's formed_at_pos, or throughout if that side has no lines) or where the deciding price is NaN (the line state is left unchanged — it keeps waiting);
  • breakout_up_level / breakout_down_level — at event bars only, the broken line's value projected to the break bar; NaN elsewhere.

detect_trendline_retest

from price_action import detect_trendline_retest

detect_trendline_retest(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    trendlines: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    retest_tolerance: float = 0.002,
    break_mode: str = 'close',
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect the first retest of each broken trendline.

A line's breakout is found first (by the same rule and break_mode as detect_trendline_breakout). Its retest is then the first bar strictly after the breakout bar whose range overlaps the band [v*(1-retest_tolerance), v*(1+retest_tolerance)], where v is the line projected to that bar — that is, low[t] <= band_upper and high[t] >= band_lower. Because the line keeps extending, v drifts with the slope and generally differs from the value at the break bar (the defining contrast with a horizontal level). A touch on the breakout bar itself does not count. Every line that broke retests at most once, and there is no cap on how many broken lines a side accumulates. With retest_tolerance=0 the band collapses to the line and an exact touch is required. Prices are assumed positive for the band definition; for a negative projected value the two bounds invert arithmetically (not special-cased).

The values DataFrame shares df's index and has four float64 columns:

  • retest_up / retest_down — 1.0 at a bar where at least one up-broken resistance (down-broken support) line is retested, 0.0 at bars with no such retest, and NaN during that direction's warm-up (mirroring the breakout warm-up: before the first resistance / support line's formed_at_pos, or throughout if that side has no lines) or where the deciding high / low is NaN (line state unchanged);
  • retest_up_level / retest_down_level — at event bars only, the first-formed broken line's value projected to the retest bar (the earliest table row among those retested); NaN elsewhere.

Because breakouts are computed internally, NaN deciding-price bars only delay a breakout (and hence its retest) rather than cancelling it.

retest_tolerancefloat0.002Relative half-width of the retest band (0.002 == 0.2%). Must be >= 0 and not NaN.
break_modestr'close'"close" (default) or "wick" — used for the internal breakout detection.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
Returns

A PAResult named "trendline_retest".

Output columns

retest_up_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined)
retest_downevent flag (0/1, NaN during warm-up)
retest_down_levellevel / position (NaN except where defined)

detect_trendlines

from price_action import detect_trendlines

detect_trendlines(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    swings: PAResult | pd.DataFrame,
    side: str = 'both',
    method: str = 'pivot_pair',
    touch_tolerance: float = 0.001,
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
    right: int | None = None,
) -> PAResult

Detect diagonal trendlines by pairing consecutive same-side swing pivots.

Walking swing confirmations in bar order, the detector keeps the most recently confirmed swing high and swing low. When a new swing low confirms, it is paired with the previous confirmed swing low: if the new pivot price is strictly greater than the previous one, an ascending support line is drawn through the two (a strictly higher low). When a new swing high confirms, it pairs with the previous swing high: strictly lower than the previous draws a descending resistance line. Equal prices draw nothing (tie handling is strict), but the new pivot still becomes the reference for the next comparison. Every qualifying consecutive pair emits a row, so three rising lows yield two support rows sharing the middle pivot as an anchor.

side selects which lines are computed ("support", "resistance", or "both"). When "both", a bar confirming both a swing high and a swing low can emit a resistance and a support row on the same bar; the resistance row is emitted first (deterministic table order).

method picks the geometry, never the trigger. Which rows are emitted, and when, is identical for both methods — the pivot pair described above gates emission and nothing else. What changes is the line drawn:

  • "pivot_pair" (default): the straight two-point line through the two pivots. anchor1_price / anchor2_price are the pivot prices and slope is (anchor2_price - anchor1_price) / (anchor2_pos - anchor1_pos). Recorded as metadata["method"] = "consecutive_pivot_pair" (unchanged from earlier releases) with metadata["geometry"] = "two_point".
  • "fit": a line fitted to every bar of the window [anchor1_pos .. formed_at_pos] (inclusive), using the window's lows for a support line and its highs for a resistance line, subject to the hard constraint that the line never crosses price — at or below every low, at or above every high. anchor1_price / anchor2_price become the fitted line's values at those two positions and slope the fitted slope (still price per bar position); the anchor positions and formed_at* are untouched. Recorded as metadata["method"] = "constrained_fit", metadata["geometry"] = "fitted_window".
The fit is solved in **closed form**, not searched: the intercept is pinned
to the window's extremum (lowest low / highest high, ties to the earliest
bar), which turns the constraint into an exact feasible slope interval
``[L, U]`` and the objective into a convex parabola, so the constrained
optimum is the anchored least-squares slope **clamped** into that interval
(``metadata["fit_solver"] = "closed_form"``). Being one straight-line
expression it is exact and bit-reproducible -- no iteration budget, no
feasibility tolerance. :func:`~price_action.trendlines._fit._fit_window`
derives it step by step. ``NaN`` bars are excluded from the fit; a window
with no usable price at all falls back to the two-point geometry, and one
with a single usable price yields the flat line through it.

Because the fit answers to the window and not to the pair, a **support
line's slope may be zero or negative** (and a resistance line's zero or
positive). That is deliberate and not filtered: the pair gates emission,
the fit is the geometry.

Quality columns (both methods). Every row also carries touches, score and body_cross, measured over the same window against the row's own line, projected exactly as the breakout/retest machine projects it. They are computed once at formation and frozen with the rest of the row, are never used to filter rows, and are not machine inputs — downstream code is free to ignore or threshold them. _window_quality defines all three; touch_tolerance is the relative band width the touches count uses.

A NaN swing event is treated as no confirmation: it never becomes an anchor and never updates the running reference (metadata["nan_swing_policy"] = "treated_as_no_swing").

Resolving pivot positions. This is the one detector that needs the pivot positions, not just the confirmation bars, and there are two ways to get them (metadata["position_source"] records which was used):

  • "pos_columns": the swings frame carries swing_high_pos and swing_low_pos — as detect_swings_zigzag emits — and the position is read straight off the confirmation bar. This is the only workable source for a variable-delay engine. metadata["right"] is then None (there is no single lag), and a right alongside the columns raises — whether it arrives as the argument or inside the swings metadata: the columns contradict any fixed lag, so a silent preference between two conflicting sources would be the wrong answer either way. Each value read must be a finite, whole, non-negative position no later than its own confirmation bar, or the frame is rejected.
  • "right": no position columns, so a pivot's position is confirmation_bar - right, the fractal engine's fixed lag. When swings is a PAResult, right is read from its metadata; a right argument may be omitted or must match (a conflicting value raises). When swings is a raw DataFrame (no metadata), right is required.
Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
dfpd.DataFrame—OHLCV dataframe. Its index and column schema are used throughout; the resolved open / high / low / close values feed the method="fit" geometry and the quality columns.

sidestr'both'"support", "resistance", or "both" (default).
methodstr'pivot_pair'"pivot_pair" (default, the two-point line) or "fit" (the constrained windowed fit).
touch_tolerancefloat0.001Relative band width for the touches count (0.001 == 0.1%). Must be >= 0 and not NaN.
columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides.
rightint | NoneNoneThe swing confirmation lag. Optional (and validated to match) for a PAResult; required for a raw DataFrame; rejected when the swings frame carries the position columns. Must be an integer (NumPy ints accepted, bool rejected) and >= 0.
Returns

A PAResult named "trendlines" whose values is the trendline table described in the module docstring.

utilities

Datasets, visualization and core plumbing · 13 names

Two utilities sit beside the detectors. load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500, seed=42, freq="1h", start="2024-01-01") returns a deterministic synthetic frame: a seeded random walk whose drift shifts across six regimes, with occasional larger shocks that seed gaps, internally consistent candles, strictly positive volume, five float64 columns and a DatetimeIndex. The same arguments always give a bit-identical frame, which is what makes it useful for examples and tests; it is not market data and describes no instrument. plot_price_action(df, results=(), columns=None, title=None) draws a plotly candlestick chart with one overlay per PAResult, chosen by result.name, and returns the Figure without ever calling .show(). Plotly is the optional viz extra (pip install -e ".[viz]"), imported only when the function is called; without it the call raises an ImportError that names the extra. The layer is presentation only — it reads values and metadata and runs no detection logic of its own. It knows 30 result names; premium_discount is refused with its own message because a 0–1 position cannot share a price axis, an unknown name raises ValueError listing the supported ones, and a non-PAResult item raises TypeError. Swing markers are drawn at the pivot bar for readability, although the detection bar is the confirmation bar.

The plumbing is what the detectors are built on. PAResult is the (name, values, metadata) container. OHLCV_COLUMNS lists the five canonical names, and ColumnMap — a Mapping[str, str] alias — maps them to a frame's own labels. resolve_columns(df, columns, required) returns the full five-name map, raising ValueError for an unknown canonical name and MissingColumnError for an absent required column. validate_ohlcv is the validator every detector calls: it resolves the map, requires at least min_rows rows (default 1), refuses duplicated or non-numeric required columns, optionally requires volume, and checks candle consistency only with check_sanity=True. validate_min_rows is the row-count step it runs; validate_columns is a separate plain label check (no column mapping, and a TypeError for a non-DataFrame) that no detector calls. Direction is an enum with BULLISH = 1, BEARISH = -1 and NEUTRAL = 0, the same encoding the signed series use, though no detector returns its members — outputs are plain float64. ColumnMap, validate_columns and validate_min_rows are exported from price_action.core, the rest from the top-level package.

The exception hierarchy is small. PriceActionError is the base; MissingColumnError (with .missing and .required) and InsufficientDataError (with .available and .required) subclass it. Everything else the library refuses is a built-in exception: an invalid parameter, a duplicated column label or a malformed swings or table input raises ValueError; a non-numeric column, a wrongly typed PAResult field, a non-PAResult passed to plot_price_action and the few boolean flags that are type-checked (wick_only, join_consecutive, require_bos) raise TypeError. Catching PriceActionError alone therefore catches only the missing-column and too-few-rows cases.

When to reach for this module: a reproducible frame to try the detectors on, a quick visual check of what they found, and the validation and column-mapping helpers for building a detector of your own on the same contract.

load_sample_ohlcv

from price_action import load_sample_ohlcv

load_sample_ohlcv(
    n_bars: int = 500,
    seed: int = 42,
    freq: str = '1h',
    start: str = '2024-01-01',
) -> pd.DataFrame

Generate a deterministic synthetic OHLCV frame for demos and tests.

The close price follows a geometric-ish random walk whose per-bar drift shifts between a handful of regimes (up-trend, down-trend, range), so the series produces the swings, breaks, and gaps the detectors are meant to find. Each candle is built to be internally consistent (high >= max(open, close) >= min(open, close) >= low) with strictly positive volume, and the frame carries a DatetimeIndex starting at start spaced by freq.

The output is a pure function of the arguments: the same (n_bars, seed, freq, start) always yields a bit-identical frame, and changing seed changes the path.

.. warning:

The returned data is **synthetic** -- a seeded random walk, not real
market data. It exists only to exercise the library in examples and
tests and must never be treated as, or analysed as, a real instrument.
Parameters
nametypedefaultdescription
n_barsint500Number of bars (rows) to generate. Must be >= 1.
seedint42Seed for numpy.random.default_rng; fixes the entire path.
freqstr'1h'Pandas frequency string for the index spacing (e.g. "1h", "15min", "1D").
startstr'2024-01-01'Timestamp of the first bar, parsed by pandas.Timestamp.
Returns

An n_bars-row dataframe with canonical lowercase columns open, high, low, close, volume (all float64) and a DatetimeIndex.

Raises
ValueErrorIf n_bars < 1.
Example
# a deterministic, seeded synthetic frame — NOT market data

df = pa.load_sample_ohlcv(n_bars=500)
df.shape                   # (500, 5)
df.columns.tolist()        # ['open', 'high', 'low', 'close', 'volume']
df.index[0], df.index[-1]  # 2024-01-01 00:00:00 … 2024-01-21 19:00:00

plot_price_action

from price_action import plot_price_action

plot_price_action(
    df: pd.DataFrame,
    results: Iterable[PAResult] = (),
    columns: ColumnMap | None = None,
    title: str | None = None,
) -> Figure

Render a candlestick chart with detector overlays and return the Figure.

A base candlestick is drawn from df (its columns resolved through columns and validated as OHLCV). Each PAResult in results is then overlaid according to result.name.

Structure.

  • "swings" — triangle markers at each confirmed swing, drawn at the pivot bar's position and price (pivot = confirmation bar t minus the right lookahead read from result.metadata) for readability; triangle-down above swing highs, triangle-up below swing lows. Note the detection bar is the confirmation bar, not the pivot — the marker is merely placed at the pivot so it sits on the extremum. If metadata lacks right the marker is placed at the confirmation bar instead. When the frame carries swing_high_pos / swing_low_pos, those recorded positions are preferred over the t - right derivation.
  • "zigzag_swings" — the same triangle conventions, but the pivot bar is read from the swing_high_pos / swing_low_pos columns the zigzag engine publishes at its confirmation bars. (The two engines differ only in where the pivot position comes from: fractal swings derive it from metadata["right"], the zigzag reads it from the *_pos columns, because its confirmation delay is not fixed.)
  • "bos" / "choch" — vertical text labels ("BOS↑", "BOS↓", "CHoCH↑", "CHoCH↓") at each event bar, at the broken level's price.
  • "market_structure" — small HH / LH / HL / LL text labels at each classified swing, drawn at the pivot bar (confirmation bar t minus the right lookahead from metadata["swings_metadata"], falling back to the confirmation bar if absent), at the pivot bar's high for the high-channel labels and its low for the low-channel labels — consistent with the swings markers.

Candle patterns ("candle_direction", "doji", "engulfing", "pin_bar" — single per-bar Series).

  • Small markers at every firing bar: a triangle-up at the bar's low for bullish events, a triangle-down at the bar's high for bearish ones. Signed (direction="both") series are split by sign; a directional series (metadata["direction"] of "bullish" / "bearish") is all one side even though its events are 1.0.
  • "doji" has no direction, so its events are drawn as neutral hollow circles at the bar's low.

Chart patterns.

  • "double_top" / "double_bottom" / "head_and_shoulders" / "inverse_head_and_shoulders" — a short text label ("DT", "DB", "H&S", "iH&S") at the break bar, at the neckline price, plus a short horizontal neckline segment ending at that bar. The segment's length is the fixed cosmetic _SEGMENT_LOOKBACK (10 bars) — the detectors publish no neckline start position, so it is a readability aid, not a claim about the pattern's extent. The *_level column (the pattern's extremum) is not drawn.
  • "range" — one translucent rectangle per active stretch: each maximal run of contiguous range_active == 1.0 bars sharing one (range_lower, range_upper) band (the bounds are frozen while a range is active, so a change in them starts a new rectangle).

Levels and trendlines.

  • "support_resistance" (level table) — one horizontal segment per row, from the row's formed_at_pos to the last bar of the chart, coloured by side.
  • "trendlines" (trendline table) — one solid segment per row from (anchor1_pos, anchor1_price) to the line's value at formed_at_pos, plus a dashed projection from there to the last bar. The line is evaluated with the library's canonical projection anchor2_price + slope * (t - anchor2_pos), the same formula the breakout/retest machine uses. Coloured by side.
  • "level_breakout" / "level_retest" / "trendline_breakout" / "trendline_retest" — triangle markers at each event bar, at the price carried by the matching *_level column; breakouts and retests get distinct colours.

Smart money concepts.

  • "fvg" — one translucent rectangle per gap event, spanning the zone [fvg_lower, fvg_upper] and extending in x from the event bar to the last bar of the chart (a research-visualisation convention: the per-bar detector tracks no fill/mitigation, so zones are drawn open-ended). Green for bullish events, red for bearish.
  • "order_blocks" — one translucent rectangle per order block, from the ob_*_upper / ob_*_lower bounds, likewise extended to the last bar, in colours distinct from the FVG zones.
  • "fvg_zones" / "ob_zones" / "breaker_blocks" (zone tables) — one translucent rectangle per row, from formed_at_pos to the last bar between lower and upper, with a distinct colour pair per table.
  • "fvg_mitigation" / "ob_mitigation" — hollow square markers at each mitigation bar, at the threshold price in the matching *_level column.
  • "liquidity_sweep" — an x marker at each sweep, at the swept level's price.
  • "equal_levels" — a marker plus a short horizontal segment at each equal-high / equal-low event, at eqh_level / eql_level, the segment again a fixed _SEGMENT_LOOKBACK cosmetic length.
  • "ote" — per side, two thin band lines (ote_*_upper and ote_*_lower) with a translucent fill between them, drawn only on the bars where the band exists; bars without a band are NaN, so plotly breaks both the lines and the fill there. The ote_* in-band flag is not drawn — the candles show where price sits inside the band.

"premium_discount" is deliberately not renderable: it reports a 0-1 position inside the dealing range, not a price, so it cannot share the candlestick axis (see _NON_PRICE_RESULTS).

The function never calls .show(); it returns the assembled Figure for the caller to display or export.

Parameters

columnsColumnMap | NoneNoneOptional canonical-to-actual column overrides for df.
titlestr | NoneNoneOptional chart title.
Returns

A plotly Figure.

Raises

Example

Container for the output of a single price-action computation.

Per-bar detectors return a pandas.Series (one value per source row), while zone/box detectors return a pandas.DataFrame (one row per detected structure). Both are accepted here.
